text: Well, two leading national news networks have both said the president’s characterization of my health-care plan is incorrect. One called it fiction. The other called it untrue.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Mr. President?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: In all due respect, I’m not so sure it’s credible to quote leading news organizations about — oh, never mind. Anyway, let me quote the Lewin report. The Lewin report is a group of folks who are not politically affiliated. They analyzed the senator’s plan. It cost $1.2 trillion.

speaker: John Kerry
text: The president just said that government-run health care results in poor quality.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Mr. President?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Talk about the VA: We’ve increased VA funding by $22 billion in the four years since I’ve been president. That’s twice the amount that my predecessor increased VA funding.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Mr. President, the next question is to you. We all know that Social Security is running out of money, and it has to be fixed. You have proposed to fix it by letting people put some of the money collected to pay benefits into private savings accounts. But the critics are saying that’s going to mean finding $1 trillion over the next 10 years to continue paying benefits as those accounts are being set up.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: First, let me make sure that every senior listening today understands that when we’re talking about reforming Social Security, that they’ll still get their checks.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Senator Kerry?

speaker: John Kerry
text: You just heard the president say that young people ought to be able to take money out of Social Security and put it in their own accounts.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Let me just stay on Social Security with a new question for Senator Kerry, because, Senator Kerry, you have just said you will not cut benefits.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Not at all. Absolutely not, Bob. This is the same thing we heard — remember, I appeared on “Meet the Press” with Tim Russert in 1990-something. We heard the same thing. We fixed it.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Mr. President?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: He forgot to tell you he voted to tax Social Security benefits more than one time. I didn’t hear any plan to fix Social Security. I heard more of the same.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Let’s go to a new question, Mr. President.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: I see it as a serious problem. I see it as a security issue, I see it as an economic issue, and I see it as a human-rights issue.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Time’s up.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Let me just answer one part of the last question quickly, and then I’ll come to immigration.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Well, to say that the borders are not as protected as they were prior to September the 11th shows he doesn’t know the borders. They’re much better protected today than they were when I was the governor of Texas.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Four thousand people a day are coming across the border.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Next question to you, Senator Kerry.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Well, I’m glad you raised that question.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Actually, Mitch McConnell had a minimum-wage plan that I supported that would have increased the minimum wage.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Mr. President, I want to go back to something Senator Kerry said earlier tonight and ask a follow-up of my own. He said — and this will be a new question to you — he said that you had never said whether you would like to overturn Roe v. Wade. So I’d ask you directly, would you like to?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: What he’s asking me is, will I have a litmus test for my judges? And the answer is, no, I will not have a litmus test. I will pick judges who will interpret the Constitution, but I’ll have no litmus test.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Senator Kerry, you’d like to respond?

speaker: John Kerry
text: Is that a new question or a 30-second question?

speaker: Schieffer
text: That’s a new question for Senator — for President Bush.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Which time limit. . .

speaker: Schieffer
text: You have 90 seconds.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Thank you very much.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Two things. One, he clearly has a litmus test for his judges, which I disagree with.

speaker: John Kerry
text: You don’t measure it by a percentage increase. Mr. President, you measure it by whether you’re getting the job done.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right, let’s go to another question. And it is to Senator Kerry.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Well, I think the fact that they’re facing these repeated call-ups, some of them two and three deployments, and there’s a stop- loss policy that prevents people from being able to get out when their time was up, is a reflection of the bad judgment this president exercised in how he has engaged in the world and deployed our forces.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Mr. President?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: The best way to take the pressure off our troops is to succeed in Iraq, is to train Iraqis so they can do the hard work of democracy, is to give them a chance to defend their country, which is precisely what we’re doing. We’ll have 125,000 troops trained by the end of this year.

speaker: John Kerry
text: I have never suggested a test where we turn over our security to any nation. In fact, I’ve said the opposite: I will never turn the security of the United States over to any nation. No nation will ever have a veto over us.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: In 1990, there was a vast coalition put together to run Saddam Hussein out of Kuwait. The international community, the international world said this is the right thing to do, but when it came time to authorize the use of force on the Senate floor, my opponent voted against the use of force.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Mr. President, new question, two minutes.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Actually, I made my intentions — made my views clear. I did think we ought to extend the assault weapons ban, and was told the fact that the bill was never going to move, because Republicans and Democrats were against the assault weapon ban, people of both parties. I believe law-abiding citizens ought to be able to own a gun. I believe in background checks at gun shows or anywhere to make sure that guns don’t get in the hands of people that shouldn’t have them.

speaker: John Kerry
text: I believe it was a failure of presidential leadership not to reauthorize the assault weapons ban.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Let’s go to a new question. For you, Senator Kerry, two minutes.

speaker: John Kerry
text: No, Bob, regrettably, we have not moved far enough along.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Mr. President?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Well, first of all, it is just not true that I haven’t met with the Black Congressional Caucus. I met with the Black Congressional Caucus at the White House.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Mr. President, let’s go to a new question.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Senator Kerry?

speaker: John Kerry
text: Well, I respect everything that the president has said and certainly respect his faith. I think it’s important and I share it. I think that he just said that freedom is a gift from the Almighty.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Senator Kerry, after 9/11 — and this is a new question for you — it seemed to me that the country came together as I’ve never seen it come together since World War II. But some of that seems to have melted away. I think it’s fair to say we’ve become pretty polarized, perhaps because of the political season.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Very much so.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Mr. President?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: My biggest disappointment in Washington is how partisan the town is. I had a record of working with Republicans and Democrats as the governor of Texas, and I was hopeful I’d be able to do the same thing.

speaker: Schieffer
text: We’ve come, gentlemen, to our last question. And it occurred to me as I came to this debate tonight that the three of us share something. All three of us are surrounded by very strong women. We’re all married to strong women. Each of us have two daughters that make us very proud.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: To listen to them.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Senator Kerry?

speaker: John Kerry
text: Well, I guess the president and you and I are three examples of lucky people who married up.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Well, gentlemen, that brings us to the closing statements.

speaker: John Kerry
text: My fellow Americans, as you heard from Bob Schieffer a moment ago, America is being tested by division. More than ever, we need to be united as a country.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Mr. President?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: In the Oval Office, there’s a painting by a friend of Laura and mine named — by Tom Lee. And it’s a West Texas painting, a painting of a mountain scene.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Thank you, Mr. President.

speaker: Cheney
text: Gwen, I want to thank you, and I want to thank the folks here at Case Western Reserve for hosting this tonight. It’s a very important event, and they’ve done a superb job of putting it together.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, you have 90 seconds to respond.

speaker: Edwards
text: Thank you.

speaker: Ifill
text: You have 30 seconds to respond, Mr. Vice President.

speaker: Cheney
text: We’ve made significant progress in Iraq. We’ve stood up a new government that’s been in power now only 90 days. The notion of additional troops is talked about frequently, but the point of success in Iraq will be reached when we have turned governance over to the Iraqi people; they have been able to establish a democratic government. They’re well on their way to doing that. They will have free elections next January for the first time in history.

speaker: Ifill
text: You have 30 seconds, Senator.

speaker: Ifill
text: Time for a new question but the same topic. And this time to you, Senator Edwards.

speaker: Edwards
text: Here’s what it means: It means that Saddam Hussein needed to be confronted. John Kerry and I have consistently said that. That’s why we voted for the resolution. But it also means it needed to be done the right way.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, you have 90 seconds to respond.

speaker: Cheney
text: The senator has got his facts wrong. I have not suggested there’s a connection between Iraq and 9/11, but there’s clearly an established Iraqi track record with terror.

speaker: Ifill
text: You will respond to that topic, but first I want to ask you for two minutes, Vice President Cheney.

speaker: Cheney
text: Gwen, we’ve never let up on Osama bin Laden from day one. We’ve actively and aggressively pursued him. We’ve captured or killed thousands of Al Qaida in various places around the world and especially in Afghanistan. We’ll continue to very aggressively pursue him, and I’m confident eventually we’ll get him.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, you have 90 seconds.

speaker: Edwards
text: Someone did get it wrong. But it wasn’t John Kerry and John Edwards. They got it wrong. When we had Osama bin Laden cornered, they left the job to the Afghan warlords. They then diverted their attention from the very people who attacked us, who were at the center of the war on terror, and so Osama bin Laden is still at large. Now, I want to go back to something the vice president said just a minute ago, because these distortions are continuing.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, 30 seconds.

speaker: Cheney
text: Twenty years ago we had a similar situation in El Salvador. We had — guerrilla insurgency controlled roughly a third of the country, 75,000 people dead, and we held free elections. I was there as an observer on behalf of the Congress.

speaker: Edwards
text: The vice president just said that we should focus on state sponsors of terrorism. Iran has moved forward with its nuclear weapons program. They’re more dangerous today than they were four years ago.

speaker: Ifill
text: New question to you, Senator Edwards, but I don’t want to let go of the global test question first, because…

speaker: Ifill
text: … I want people to understand exactly what it is, as you said, that Senator Kerry did say.

speaker: Edwards
text: Well, let me say, first, he said in the same segment — I don’t remember precisely where it was connected with what you just read — but he said, point blank, “We will never give anyone a veto over the security of the United States of America.”

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, you have 90 seconds to respond.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, Gwen, the 90 percent figure is just dead wrong. When you include the Iraqi security forces that have suffered casualties, as well as the allies, they’ve taken almost 50 percent of the casualties in operations in Iraq, which leaves the U.S. with 50 percent, not 90 percent.

speaker: Edwards
text: May I respond briefly?

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, you have 30 seconds.

speaker: Cheney
text: Your rhetoric, Senator, would be a lot more credible if there was a record to back it up. There isn’t. And you cannot use “talk tough” during the course of a 90-minute debate in a presidential campaign to obscure a 30-year record in the United States Senate and, prior to that by John Kerry, who has consistently come down on the wrong side of all the major defense issues that he’s faced as a public official.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, a new question for you. You have two minutes to respond.

speaker: Cheney
text: I’m saying specifically that I don’t believe he has the qualities we need in a commander in chief because I don’t think, based on his record, that he would pursue the kind of aggressive policies that need to be pursued if we’re going to defeat these terrorists. We need to battle them overseas so we don’t have to battle them here at home.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, you have 90 seconds to respond.

speaker: Edwards
text: Thank you.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, you have 30 seconds.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, Gwen, I think the record speaks for itself. These are two individuals who have been for the war when the headlines were good and against it when their poll ratings were bad.

speaker: Ifill
text: And 30 seconds…

speaker: Edwards
text: John Kerry has been absolutely clear and consistent from the beginning that we must stay focused on the people who attacked us; that Saddam Hussein was a threat that needed to be addressed directly; that the weapons inspectors needed to have time to do their job.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, new question to you, and you have two minutes to respond.

speaker: Edwards
text: Well, let’s start with what we know. What we know is that the president and the vice president have not done the work to build the coalition that we need — dramatically different than the first Gulf War. We know that they haven’t done it, and we know they can’t do it.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, you have 90 seconds.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, Gwen, it’s hard to know where to start; there are so many inaccuracies there.

speaker: Edwards
text: Thank you.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President?

speaker: Cheney
text: Classic example. He won’t count the sacrifice and the contribution of Iraqi allies. It’s their country. They’re in the fight. They’re increasingly the ones out there putting their necks on the line to take back their country from the terrorists and the old regime elements that are still left. They’re doing a superb job. And for you to demean their sacrifices strikes me as…

speaker: Edwards
text: Oh, I’m not…

speaker: Cheney
text: … as beyond…

speaker: Edwards
text: I’m not demeaning…

speaker: Cheney
text: It is indeed. You suggested…

speaker: Edwards
text: No, sir, I did not…

speaker: Cheney
text: … somehow they shouldn’t count, because you want to be able to say that the Americans are taking 90 percent of the sacrifice. You cannot succeed in this effort if you’re not willing to recognize the enormous contribution the Iraqis are increasingly making to their own future.

speaker: Ifill
text: New question, similar topic, because I want to circle back to a question which I’m not quite certain we got an answer to.

speaker: Ifill
text: It’s a question of American intelligence.

speaker: Edwards
text: Well, let me speak, first of all, to what the vice president just said, and then I’ll answer that question.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President? CHENEY: Gwen, the story that appeared today about this report is one I asked for. I ask an awful lot of questions as part of my job as vice president. A CIA spokesman was quoted in that story as saying they had not yet reached the bottom line and there is still debate over this question of the relationship between Zarqawi and Saddam Hussein.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, in June of 2000 when you were still CEO of Halliburton, you said that U.S. businesses should be allowed to do business with Iran because, quote, “Unilateral sanctions almost never work.”

speaker: Cheney
text: No, I do not. And, Gwen, at the time, I was talking specifically about this question of unilateral sanctions.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards?

speaker: Edwards
text: Well, the vice president talks about there being a member, or someone associated with Al Qaida, in Iraq. There are 60 countries who have members of Al Qaida in them.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President?

speaker: Cheney
text: I can respond, Gwen, but it’s going to take more than 30 seconds.

speaker: Ifill
text: Well, that’s all you’ve got.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, the reason they keep mentioning Halliburton is because they’re trying to throw up a smokescreen. They know the charges are false.

speaker: Ifill
text: Thirty seconds.

speaker: Edwards
text: These are the facts.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, as we wrap up the foreign policy part of this, I do want to talk to you about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

speaker: Edwards
text: Well, first of all, I do agree that we’ve been largely absent, not entirely absent, but largely absent from the peace-making process over the last four years.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, 90 seconds.

speaker: Cheney
text: Gwen, I want to go back to the last comment, and then I’ll come back to Israel-Palestine.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, it’s your turn to use 30 seconds for a complicated response…

speaker: Edwards
text: That was a complete distortion of my record. I know that won’t come as a shock.

speaker: Ifill
text: Thirty seconds.

speaker: Cheney
text: Oh, I think his record speaks for itself. And frankly, it’s not very distinguished.

speaker: Ifill
text: In that case, we’ll move on to domestic matters. And this question, I believe, goes to Senator — to Vice President Cheney.

speaker: Cheney
text: I think it goes to Senator Edwards.

speaker: Ifill
text: It goes to the Senator. I see you. I just asked him about Israel, even though we didn’t actually talk about it much.

speaker: Cheney
text: I concede the point.

speaker: Edwards
text: No, I did talk about it, Israel. He’s the one who didn’t talk about it.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, the Census Bureau ranked Cleveland as the biggest poor city in the country, 31 percent jobless rate.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, Gwen, there are several things that I think need to be done and are being done.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, you have 90 seconds.

speaker: Edwards
text: Gwen, your question was about jobs?

speaker: Ifill
text: It was about jobs, and it was about poverty.

speaker: Edwards
text: I thought it was about jobs and poverty. I hope we get a chance to talk about education, but that’s what the vice president talked about.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President?

speaker: Cheney
text: Gwen, we’ve got 111 million American taxpayers that have benefited from our income tax cuts.

speaker: Ifill
text: Thirty seconds.

speaker: Edwards
text: The vice president and president like to talk about their experience on the campaign trail. Millions of people have lost their jobs. Millions have fallen into poverty. Family incomes are down, while the cost of everything is going up.

speaker: Ifill
text: This next question goes to you, Senator Edwards.

speaker: Edwards
text: Because we will do what they’ve not done. You know, if you look at what’s happened over the last four years, we have gone from a $5 trillion projected surplus when George Bush took office to a $3 trillion projected deficit.

speaker: Ifill
text: You have 90 seconds, Mr. Vice President.

speaker: Cheney
text: Gwen, the Kerry record on taxes is one basically of voting for a large number of tax increases — 98 times in the United States Senate.

speaker: Ifill
text: Thirty seconds, Senator Edwards.

speaker: Edwards
text: We are committed to cutting back anything in our programs that need to be cut back to get us back on a path to fiscal responsibility.

speaker: Ifill
text: You have 30 seconds, Mr. Vice President.

speaker: Cheney
text: Yesterday, the president signed an extension of middle- class tax cuts, the 10 percent bracket, the marriage penalty relief and the increase in the child tax credit.

speaker: Ifill
text: The next question goes to you, Mr. Vice President.

speaker: Cheney
text: Gwen, you’re right, four years ago in this debate, the subject came up. And I said then and I believe today that freedom does mean freedom for everybody. People ought to be free to choose any arrangement they want. It’s really no one else’s business.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, 90 seconds.

speaker: Edwards
text: Yes. Let me say first, on an issue that the vice president said in his last answer before we got to this question, talking about tax policy, the country needs to know that under what they have put in place and want to put in place, a millionaire sitting by their swimming pool, collecting their statements to see how much money they’re making, make their money from dividends, pays a lower tax rate than the men and women who are receiving paychecks for serving on the ground in Iraq.

speaker: Ifill
text: New question, but same subject.

speaker: Edwards
text: No. I think we’ve both said the same thing all along.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, you have 90 seconds.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, Gwen, let me simply thank the senator for the kind words he said about my family and our daughter. I appreciate that very much.

speaker: Ifill
text: That’s it?

speaker: Cheney
text: That’s it.

speaker: Ifill
text: OK, then we’ll move on to the next question.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, Gwen…

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President?

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards?

speaker: Edwards
text: Yes. Well let me say, first of all, I’m proud of the work I did on behalf of kids and families against big insurance companies, big drug companies and big HMOs.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, new question to you, same topic. Do you feel personally attacked when Vice President Cheney talks about liability reform and tort reform and the president talks about having a trial lawyer on the ticket?

speaker: Edwards
text: Am I personally attacked?

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President?

speaker: Cheney
text: Gwen, we think lawsuit abuse is a serious problem in this country. We think we badly need tort reform.

speaker: Ifill
text: You have 30 seconds to respond.

speaker: Edwards
text: Well, first of all, I have paid all the taxes that I owe.

speaker: Ifill
text: Thirty seconds, Mr. Vice President.

speaker: Cheney
text: We’ve done a lot to reduce the cost of health care. The Medicare drug benefit that we’ll be providing to seniors beginning in ’06 will provide upwards to $1,300 a year to help them buy prescription drugs.

speaker: Ifill
text: I will talk to you about health care, Mr. Vice President. You have two minutes. But in particular, I want to talk to you about AIDS, and not about AIDS in China or Africa, but AIDS right here in this country, where black women between the ages of 25 and 44 are 13 times more likely to die of the disease than their counterparts.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, this is a great tragedy, Gwen, when you think about the enormous cost here in the United States and around the world of the AIDS epidemic — pandemic, really. Millions of lives lost, millions more infected and facing a very bleak future.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, you have 90 seconds.

speaker: Edwards
text: Well, first, with respect to what’s happening in Africa and Russia and in other places around the world, the vice president spoke about the $15 billion for AIDS. John Kerry and I believe that needs to be doubled.

speaker: Ifill
text: OK, we’ll move on.

speaker: Edwards
text: The American people want in their president and in their vice president basically three things: They want to know that their president and their vice president will keep them safe. They want to know that they have good judgment. And they want to know that you’ll tell them the truth.

speaker: Cheney
text: You want me to answer a question about his qualifications?

speaker: Ifill
text: That was the question.

speaker: Ifill
text: You have 30 seconds, if you’d like to respond to that.

speaker: Edwards
text: I think the most important thing I’ve learned from this process is what I now know about John Kerry. I knew him before. I know him better now.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, I clearly believe that George W. Bush would be a better commander in chief. He’s already done it for four years.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, picking up on that, you both just sang the praises of the tops of your ticket.

speaker: Cheney
text: Why I am different from John Edwards. Well, in some respects, I think, probably there are more similarities than there are differences in our personal story.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator Edwards, you have 90 seconds.

speaker: Edwards
text: Mr. Vice President, we were attacked. But we weren’t attacked by Saddam Hussein. And one thing that John Kerry and I would agree with you about is that it is…

speaker: Ifill
text: You just used John Kerry’s name.

speaker: Edwards
text: Oh, I’m sorry. I broke the rule.

speaker: Ifill
text: Would you like to respond? Thirty seconds.

speaker: Ifill
text: OK, we’ll move on. This goes to Senator Edwards.

speaker: Edwards
text: Well, first of all, let me say that John Kerry has — I can use his name now?

speaker: Edwards
text: OK. John Kerry has been, as have I, been completely consistent about Iraq. We’ve made very clear from the beginning — and not an afterthought; we said it at the time — that we had to confront Saddam Hussein and that we had to have a coalition and a plan to be successful.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President? CHENEY: Well, Gwen, I can think of a lot of words to describe Senator Kerry’s position on Iraq; “consistent” is not one of them.

speaker: Ifill
text: You have 30 seconds if you choose.

speaker: Edwards
text: Yes, but they didn’t fund the mandates that they put on the schools all over this country. That’s the reason 800 teachers — one of the reasons — 800 teachers have been laid off, right here in Cleveland. One-third of our public schools are failing under this administration. Half of African-Americans are dropping out of high school. Half of Hispanic-American are dropping out of high school.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President?

speaker: Cheney
text: Gwen, No Child Left Behind, they were for it; now they’re against it. They voted for it; now they’re opposed to it.

speaker: Ifill
text: Mr. Vice President, our final — I’m sorry, you have 30 seconds, Senator Edwards.

speaker: Edwards
text: Are you sure — yes, he started. Yes, 30 seconds, please, yes.

speaker: Ifill
text: I did figure out I was wrong.

speaker: Edwards
text: Well, in fairness, if you feel like you need to go to him, we’ll — I’ll stop. IFILL: Well, I do, because we’re actually on the final question. I apologize for giving you an extra 15 seconds there. I go now to Vice President Cheney.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, I must say it’s one of the disappointments of the last four years, is that we’ve not been able to do what the president did in Texas, for example, when he was able to reach across the aisle and bring Democrats along on major issues of the day.

speaker: Ifill
text: Senator, there’s 90 seconds.

speaker: Edwards
text: Thank you.

speaker: Ifill
text: You have 30 seconds to respond to that, Mr. Vice President.

speaker: Cheney
text: Well, Gwen — I’m sorry, it’s hard to know where to start.

speaker: Ifill
text: Thirty seconds.

speaker: Edwards
text: They had a choice on allowing prescription drugs into this country from Canada, of being with the American people or with the drug companies. They were with the drug companies.

speaker: Ifill
text: As previously agreed, we’ll go to closing statements now, two minutes each.

speaker: Edwards
text: Thank you.

speaker: Ifill
text: Vice President Cheney?

speaker: Cheney
text: Gwen, I want to thank you.

speaker: Ifill
text: And with that, we come to the end of tonight’s debate.

speaker: Otis
text: Senator Kerry, after talking with several co-workers and family and friends, I asked the ones who said they were not voting for you, “Why?” They said that you were too wishy-washy.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Yes, I certainly do.

speaker: Gibson
text: Mr. President, a minute and a half.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Charlie, thank you, and thank our panelists.

speaker: Gibson
text: Mr. President, I would follow up, but we have a series of questions on Iraq, and so I will turn to the next questioner.

speaker: Dahle
text: Mr. President, yesterday in a statement you admitted that Iraq did not have weapons of mass destruction, but justified the invasion by stating, I quote, “He retained the knowledge, the materials, the means and the intent to produce weapons of mass destruction and could have passed this knowledge to our terrorist enemies.”

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Each situation is different, Robin.

speaker: Gibson
text: Senator Kerry, a minute and a half.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Robin, I’m going to answer your question.

speaker: Gibson
text: Mr. President, I do want to follow up on this one, because there were several questions from the audience along this line.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: (OFF-MIKE)

speaker: Gibson
text: Go ahead. Go ahead.

speaker: Gibson
text: Well, I was going to have you do the rebuttal on it, but you go ahead.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: You remember the last debate?

speaker: John Kerry
text: The goal of the sanctions was not to remove Saddam Hussein, it was to remove the weapons of mass destruction. And, Mr. President, just yesterday the Duelfer report told you and the whole world they worked. He didn’t have weapons of mass destruction, Mr. President. That was the objective.

speaker: Gibson
text: We’re going to have another question now on the subject of Iraq.

speaker: Baldi
text: Senator Kerry, the U.S. is preparing a new Iraq government and will proceed to withdraw U.S. troops.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Anthony, I would not. I have laid out a different plan, because the president’s plan is not working. You see that every night on television.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Two days ago in the Oval Office, I met with the finance minister from Iraq. He came to see me. And he talked about how optimistic he was and the country was about heading toward elections.

speaker: Gibson
text: Do you want to follow up, Senator?

speaker: John Kerry
text: Yes, sir, please.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: First of all, we didn’t find out he didn’t have weapons until we got there, and my opponent thought he had weapons and told everybody he thought he had weapons.

speaker: Gibson
text: The next question is for President Bush, and it comes from Nikki Washington.

speaker: Washington
text: Thank you.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: No, I appreciate that. I — listen, I — we’ve got a great country. I love our values. And I recognize I’ve made some decisions that have caused people to not understand the great values of our country.

speaker: Gibson
text: Senator Kerry, a minute and a half.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Nikki, that’s a question that’s been raised by a lot of people around the country.

speaker: Gibson
text: Mr. President?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: I remember sitting in the White House looking at those generals, saying, “Do you have what you need in this war? Do you have what it takes?”

speaker: John Kerry
text: You rely on good military people to execute the military component of the strategy, but winning the peace is larger than just the military component.

speaker: Gibson
text: The next question is for Senator Kerry, and it comes from over here, from Randee Jacobs.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Is it Randee?

speaker: Jacobs
text: Yes, Randee.

speaker: John Kerry
text: I don’t think you can just rely on U.N. sanctions, Randee. But you’re absolutely correct, it is a threat, it’s a huge threat.

speaker: Gibson
text: Mr. President, a minute and a half.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: That answer almost made me want to scowl.

speaker: Gibson
text: We’re going to move on, Mr. President, with a question for you. And it comes from Daniel Farley.

speaker: Farley
text: Mr. President, since we continue to police the world, how do you intend to maintain our military presence without reinstituting a draft?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Yes, that’s a great question. Thanks.

speaker: Gibson
text: Senator Kerry, a minute and a half.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Daniel, I don’t support a draft.

speaker: Gibson
text: Mr. President, let’s extend for a minute…

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Let me just — I’ve got to answer this.

speaker: Gibson
text: Exactly. And with Reservists being held on duty…

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Let me answer what he just said, about around the world.

speaker: Gibson
text: Well, I want to get into the issue of the back-door draft…

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: You tell Tony Blair we’re going alone. Tell Tony Blair we’re going alone. Tell Silvio Berlusconi we’re going alone. Tell Aleksander Kwasniewski of Poland we’re going alone.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Mr. President, countries are leaving the coalition, not joining. Eight countries have left it.

speaker: Gibson
text: The next question, Senator Kerry, is for you, and it comes from Ann Bronsing, who I believe is over in this area.

speaker: Bronsing
text: Senator Kerry, we have been fortunate that there have been no further terrorist attacks on American soil since 9/11. Why do you think this is?

speaker: John Kerry
text: Thank you very much, Ann.

speaker: Gibson
text: Mr. President?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: That’s an odd thing to say, since we’ve tripled the homeland security budget from $10 billion to $30 billion.

speaker: Gibson
text: I want to extend for a minute, Senator. And I’m curious about something you said. You said, “It’s not when, but if.” You think it’s inevitable because the sense of security is a very basic thing with everybody in this country worried about their kids.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Well, the president and his experts have told America that it’s not a question of if; it’s a question of when. And I accept what the president has said. These terrorists are serious, they’re deadly, and they know nothing except trying to kill.

speaker: Gibson
text: Mr. President?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Well, we’ll talk about the tax cut for middle class here in a minute. But yes, I’m worried. I’m worried. I’m worried about our country. And all I can tell you is every day I know that there’s people working overtime, doing the very best they can. And the reason I’m worried is because there’s a vicious enemy that has an ideology of hate.

speaker: Gibson
text: Mr. President, we’re going to turn to questions now on domestic policy. And we’re going to start with health issues.

speaker: Horstman
text: Mr. President, why did you block the reimportation of safer and inexpensive drugs from Canada which would have cut 40 to 60 percent off of the cost?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: I haven’t yet. Just want to make sure they’re safe. When a drug comes in from Canada, I want to make sure it cures you and doesn’t kill you.

speaker: Gibson
text: Senator, a minute and a half.

speaker: John Kerry
text: John, you heard the president just say that he thought he might try to be for it.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: If they’re safe, they’re coming. I want to remind you that it wasn’t just my administration that made the decision on safety. President Clinton did the same thing, because we have an obligation to protect you.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Actually, Mr. President, in 1997 we fixed Medicare, and I was one of the people involved in it.

speaker: Gibson
text: The next question is for Senator Kerry. And this comes from Norma-Jean Laurent.

speaker: Laurent
text: Senator Kerry, you’ve stated your concern for the rising cost of health care, yet you chose a vice presidential candidate who has made millions of dollars successfully suing medical professionals. How do you reconcile this with the voters?

speaker: John Kerry
text: Very easily. John Edwards is the author of the Patients’ Bill of Rights. He wanted to give people rights. John Edwards and I support tort reform. We both believe that, as lawyers — I’m a lawyer, too. And I believe that we will be able to get a fix that has alluded everybody else because we know how to do it.

speaker: Gibson
text: Mr. President, a minute and a half.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Let me see where to start here.

speaker: Gibson
text: Senator Kerry, we got several questions along this line, and I’m just curious if you’d go further on what you talked about with tort reform. Would you be favoring capping awards on pain and suffering? Would you limit attorney’s fees?

speaker: John Kerry
text: A follow-up…

speaker: Gibson
text: Yes. A follow-up on this for…

speaker: John Kerry
text: Yes, I think we should look at the punitive and we should have some limitations.

speaker: Gibson
text: We’ll get to that in just a minute.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: You’re right, what does matter is a plan. He said he’s for — you’re now for capping punitive damages?

speaker: Gibson
text: The next question is for President Bush, and it comes from Matthew O’Brien.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Right, thank you for that.

speaker: Gibson
text: Senator Kerry, a minute and a half.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Let me begin by saying that my health-care plan is not what the president described. It is not a government takeover.

speaker: Gibson
text: I both — I heard you both say — I have heard you both say during the campaign, I just heard you say it, that you’re going to cut the deficit by a half in four years. But I didn’t hear one thing in the last three and a half minutes that would indicate how either one of you do that.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Well, look at the budget. One is make sure Congress doesn’t overspend.

speaker: Gibson
text: Senator Kerry, 30 seconds.

speaker: John Kerry
text: After 9/11, after the recession had ended, the president asked for another tax cut and promised 5.6 million jobs would be created. He lost 1.6 million, ladies and gentlemen. And most of that tax cut went to the wealthiest people in the country.

speaker: Gibson
text: Senator Kerry, the next question will be for you, and it comes from James Varner, who I believe is in this section.

speaker: Varner
text: Thank you.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Absolutely. Yes. Right into the camera. Yes. I am not going to raise taxes.

speaker: Gibson
text: Mr. President, 90 seconds.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: He’s just not credible when he talks about being fiscally conservative. He’s just not credible. If you look at his record in the Senate, he voted to break the caps — the spending caps — over 200 times.

speaker: Gibson
text: No, you can keep going.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Good. You looked at me like my clock was up.

speaker: Gibson
text: I’m going to come back one more time to how these numbers add up and how you can cut that deficit in half in four years, given what you’ve both said.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Well, first of all, the president’s figures of $2.2 trillion just aren’t accurate. Those are the fuzzy math figures put together by some group that works for the campaign. That’s not the number.

speaker: Gibson
text: Thirty seconds. I’m sorry, thirty seconds, Mr. President.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Yes, I mean, he’s got a record. It’s been there for 20 years. You can run, but you can’t hide. He voted 98 times to raise taxes. I mean, these aren’t make-up figures.

speaker: Gibson
text: Mr. President, the next question is for you, and it comes from James Hubb over here.

speaker: Hubb
text: Mr. President, how would you rate yourself as an environmentalist? What specifically has your administration done to improve the condition of our nation’s air and water supply?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Off-road diesel engines — we have reached an agreement to reduce pollution from off-road diesel engines by 90 percent.

speaker: Gibson
text: Senator Kerry, minute and a half.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Boy, to listen to that — the president, I don’t think, is living in a world of reality with respect to the environment.

speaker: Gibson
text: Mr. President?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Well, had we joined the Kyoto treaty, which I guess he’s referring to, it would have cost America a lot of jobs.

speaker: Gibson
text: Senator Kerry, 30 seconds.

speaker: John Kerry
text: The fact is that the Kyoto treaty was flawed. I was in Kyoto, and I was part of that. I know what happened. But this president didn’t try to fix it. He just declared it dead, ladies and gentlemen, and we walked away from the work of 160 nations over 10 years.

speaker: Gibson
text: Senator Kerry, the next question is for you. It involves jobs, which is a topic of the news today.

speaker: Barrow
text: Senator Kerry, how can the U.S. be competitive in manufacturing given — in manufacturing, excuse me — given the wage necessary and comfortably accepted for American workers to maintain the standard of living that they expect?

speaker: John Kerry
text: Jane, there are a lot of ways to be competitive. And unfortunately again I regret this administration has not seized them and embraced them. Let me give you an example.

speaker: Gibson
text: Mr. President, minute and a half.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Let me start with how to control the cost of health care: medical liability reform, for starters, which he’s opposed.

speaker: Gibson
text: Senator, I want to extend for a minute, you talk about tax credits to stop outsourcing. But when you have IBM documents that I saw recently where you can hire a programmer for $12 in China, $56 an hour here, tax credits won’t cut it.

speaker: John Kerry
text: You can’t stop all outsourcing, Charlie. I’ve never promised that. I’m not going to, because that would be pandering. You can’t.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: I own a timber company?

speaker: Gibson
text: President Bush, the next question is for you, and it comes from Rob Fowler, who I believe is over in this area.

speaker: Fowler
text: President Bush, 45 days after 9/11, Congress passed the Patriot Act, which takes away checks on law enforcement and weakens American citizens’ rights and freedoms, especially Fourth Amendment rights.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: I appreciate that.

speaker: Gibson
text: Senator Kerry, a minute and a half.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Former Governor Racicot, as chairman of the Republican Party, said he thought that the Patriot Act has to be changed and fixed.

speaker: Gibson
text: Senator Kerry, the next question is for you, and it comes from Elizabeth Long.

speaker: Long
text: Senator Kerry, thousands of people have already been cured or treated by the use of adult stem cells or umbilical cord stem cells. However, no one has been cured by using embryonic stem cells.

speaker: John Kerry
text: You know, Elizabeth, I really respect your — the feeling that’s in your question. I understand it. I know the morality that’s prompting that question, and I respect it enormously.

speaker: Gibson
text: Mr. President, a minute and a half.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Embryonic stem-cell research requires the destruction of life to create a stem cell. I’m the first president ever to allow funding — federal funding — for embryonic stem-cell research. I did to because I too hope that we’ll discover cures from the stem cells and from the research derived.

speaker: Gibson
text: Senator, 30 seconds, less extent.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Well, you talk about walking a waffle line — he says he’s allowed it, which means he’s going to allow the destruction of life up to a certain amount and then he isn’t going to allow it.

speaker: Gibson
text: Mr. President?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Let me make sure you understand my decision. Those stem- cells lines already existed. The embryo had already been destroyed prior to my decision.

speaker: Gibson
text: Mr. President, the next question is for you, and it comes from Jonathan Michaelson, over here.

speaker: Michaelson
text: Mr. President, if there were a vacancy in the Supreme Court and you had the opportunity to fill that position today, who would you choose and why?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: I’m not telling.

speaker: Gibson
text: Senator Kerry, a minute and a half.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Thank you, Charlie.

speaker: Gibson
text: Going to go to the final two questions now, and the first one will be for Senator Kerry. And this comes from Sarah Degenhart.

speaker: Degenhart
text: Senator Kerry, suppose you are speaking with a voter who believed abortion is murder and the voter asked for reassurance that his or her tax dollars would not go to support abortion, what would you say to that person?

speaker: John Kerry
text: I would say to that person exactly what I will say to you right now.

speaker: Gibson
text: Mr. President, minute and a half.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: I’m trying to decipher that.

speaker: Gibson
text: Senator, do you want to follow up? Thirty seconds.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Well, again, the president just said, categorically, my opponent is against this, my opponent is against that. You know, it’s just not that simple. No, I’m not.

speaker: Gibson
text: And 30 seconds, Mr. President.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Well, it’s pretty simple when they say: Are you for a ban on partial birth abortion? Yes or no?

speaker: Gibson
text: And the final question of the evening will be addressed to President Bush and it will come from Linda Grabel. Linda Grabel’s over here.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Put a head fake on us.

speaker: Gibson
text: I got faked out myself.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Hi, Linda.

speaker: Grabel
text: President Bush, during the last four years, you have made thousands of decisions that have affected millions of lives. Please give three instances in which you came to realize you had made a wrong decision, and what you did to correct it. Thank you.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: I have made a lot of decisions, and some of them little, like appointments to boards you never heard of, and some of them big.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: But history will look back, and I’m fully prepared to accept any mistakes that history judges to my administration, because the president makes the decisions, the president has to take the responsibility.

speaker: Gibson
text: Senator Kerry, a minute and a half.

speaker: John Kerry
text: I believe the president made a huge mistake, a catastrophic mistake, not to live up to his own standard, which was: build a true global coalition, give the inspectors time to finish their job and go through the U.N. process to its end and go to war as a last resort.

speaker: Gibson
text: Mr. President?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: He complains about the fact our troops don’t have adequate equipment, yet he voted against the $87 billion supplemental I sent to the Congress and then issued one of the most amazing quotes in political history: “I actually did vote for the $87 billion before I voted against it.”

speaker: Gibson
text: And, Senator Kerry, 30 seconds.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Not necessarily be in power, but here’s what I’ll say about the $87 billion.

speaker: Gibson
text: That’s going to conclude the questioning. We’re going to go now to closing statements, two minutes from each candidate.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Do you want to go first?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Either way.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Thank you.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Thank you, all of you, for taking part.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Charlie, thanks.

speaker: Gibson
text: Mr. President, Senator Kerry, that concludes tonight’s debate.

speaker: Moderator
text: Good evening, Mr. President, Senator Kerry.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Yes, I do.

speaker: Moderator
text: Mr. President, you have a 90-second rebuttal.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: I, too, thank the University of Miami, and say our prayers are with the good people of this state, who’ve suffered a lot.

speaker: Moderator
text: New question, Mr. President, two minutes.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: No, I don’t believe it’s going to happen. I believe I’m going to win, because the American people know I know how to lead. I’ve shown the American people I know how to lead.

speaker: Moderator
text: Ninety second response, Senator Kerry.

speaker: John Kerry
text: I believe in being strong and resolute and determined. And I will hunt down and kill the terrorists, wherever they are.

speaker: Moderator
text: New question, two minutes, Senator Kerry.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Well, where do you want me to begin?

speaker: Moderator
text: Ninety-second response, Mr. President.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: My opponent looked at the same intelligence I looked at and declared in 2002 that Saddam Hussein was a grave threat.

speaker: Moderator
text: New question, Mr. President. Two minutes.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Jim, we’ve got the capability of doing both.

speaker: Moderator
text: Senator Kerry, 90 seconds.

speaker: John Kerry
text: The president just talked about Iraq as a center of the war on terror. Iraq was not even close to the center of the war on terror before the president invaded it.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Can I respond to that?

speaker: Moderator
text: Let’s do one of these one-minute extensions. You have 30 seconds.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Thank you, sir. First of all, what my opponent wants you to forget is that he voted to authorize the use of force and now says it’s the wrong war at the wrong time at the wrong place.

speaker: Moderator
text: Thirty seconds, Senator.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Yes, we have to be steadfast and resolved, and I am. And I will succeed for those troops, now that we’re there. We have to succeed. We can’t leave a failed Iraq. But that doesn’t mean it wasn’t a mistake of judgment to go there and take the focus off of Osama bin Laden. It was. Now, we can succeed. But I don’t believe this president can. I think we need a president who has the credibility to bring the allies back to the table and to do what’s necessary to make it so America isn’t doing this alone.

speaker: Moderator
text: We’ll come back to Iraq in a moment. But I want to come back to where I began, on homeland security. This is a two-minute new question, Senator Kerry.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Jim, let me tell you exactly what I’ll do. And there are a long list of thing. First of all, what kind of mixed message does it send when you have $500 million going over to Iraq to put police officers in the streets of Iraq, and the president is cutting the COPS program in America?

speaker: Moderator
text: Ninety-second response, Mr. President.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: I don’t think we want to get to how he’s going to pay for all these promises. It’s like a huge tax gap. Anyway, that’s for another debate.

speaker: Moderator
text: Yes, let’s do a little — yes, 30 seconds.

speaker: John Kerry
text: The president just said the FBI had changed its culture. We just read on the front pages of America’s papers that there are over 100,000 hours of tapes, unlistened to. On one of those tapes may be the enemy being right the next time.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Of course we’re doing everything we can to protect America. I wake up every day thinking about how best to protect America. That’s my job.

speaker: Moderator
text: New question, Mr. President. Two minutes.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Let me first tell you that the best way for Iraq to be safe and secure is for Iraqi citizens to be trained to do the job.

speaker: Moderator
text: Ninety seconds, Senator Kerry.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Thank you, Jim.

speaker: Moderator
text: All right, go ahead. Yes, sir?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: I think it’s worthy for a follow-up.

speaker: Moderator
text: Sure, right.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: My opponent says help is on the way, but what kind of message does it say to our troops in harm’s way, “wrong war, wrong place, wrong time”? Not a message a commander in chief gives, or this is a “great diversion.”

speaker: Moderator
text: Senator Kerry, 30 seconds.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Well, you know, when I talked about the $87 billion, I made a mistake in how I talk about the war. But the president made a mistake in invading Iraq. Which is worse?

speaker: Moderator
text: All right, new question. Two minutes, Senator Kerry.

speaker: John Kerry
text: No, and they don’t have to, providing we have the leadership that we put — that I’m offering.

speaker: Moderator
text: Ninety seconds.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: That’s totally absurd. Of course, the U.N. was invited in. And we support the U.N. efforts there. They pulled out after Sergio de Mello got killed. But they’re now back in helping with elections.

speaker: Moderator
text: 30 seconds, Senator.

speaker: John Kerry
text: The United Nations, Kofi Annan offered help after Baghdad fell. And we never picked him up on that and did what was necessary to transfer authority and to transfer reconstruction. It was always American-run.

speaker: Moderator
text: Thirty seconds, Mr. President.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Well, actually, he forgot Poland. And now there’s 30 nations involved, standing side by side with our American troops.

speaker: Moderator
text: New question, Mr. President, two minutes. You have said there was a, quote, “miscalculation,” of what the conditions would be in post-war Iraq. What was the miscalculation, and how did it happen?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: No, what I said was that, because we achieved such a rapid victory, more of the Saddam loyalists were around. I mean, we thought we’d whip more of them going in.

speaker: Moderator
text: Ninety seconds, Senator Kerry.

speaker: John Kerry
text: What I think troubles a lot of people in our country is that the president has just sort of described one kind of mistake. But what he has said is that, even knowing there were no weapons of mass destruction, even knowing there was no imminent threat, even knowing there was no connection with Al Qaida, he would still have done everything the same way. Those are his words.

speaker: Moderator
text: New question. Senator Kerry, two minutes. You just — you’ve repeatedly accused President Bush — not here tonight, but elsewhere before — of not telling the truth about Iraq, essentially of lying to the American people about Iraq. Give us some examples of what you consider to be his not telling the truth.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Well, I’ve never, ever used the harshest word, as you did just then. And I try not to. I’ve been — but I’ll nevertheless tell you that I think he has not been candid with the American people. And I’ll tell you exactly how.

speaker: Moderator
text: Ninety seconds, Mr. President.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: My opponent just said something amazing. He said Osama bin Laden uses the invasion of Iraq as an excuse to spread hatred for America. Osama bin Laden isn’t going to determine how we defend ourselves.

speaker: Moderator
text: Thirty seconds. We’ll do a 30 second here.

speaker: John Kerry
text: I wasn’t misleading when I said he was a threat. Nor was I misleading on the day that the president decided to go to war when I said that he had made a mistake in not building strong alliances and that I would have preferred that he did more diplomacy.

speaker: Moderator
text: Thirty seconds, Mr. President.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: The only thing consistent about my opponent’s position is that he’s been inconsistent. He changes positions. And you cannot change positions in this war on terror if you expect to win.

speaker: Moderator
text: New question, Mr. President. Two minutes.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: You know, every life is precious. Every life matters. You know, my hardest — the hardest part of the job is to know that I committed the troops in harm’s way and then do the best I can to provide comfort for the loved ones who lost a son or a daughter or a husband or wife.

speaker: Moderator
text: Senator, 90 seconds.

speaker: John Kerry
text: I understand what the president is talking about, because I know what it means to lose people in combat. And the question, is it worth the cost, reminds me of my own thinking when I came back from fighting in that war.

speaker: Moderator
text: All right, sir, go ahead. Thirty seconds.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Yes, I understand what it means to the commander in chief. And if I were to ever say, “This is the wrong war at the wrong time at the wrong place,” the troops would wonder, how can I follow this guy?

speaker: Moderator
text: Senator Kerry, you have 30 seconds. You have 30 seconds, right. And then the president.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Secretary of State Colin Powell told this president the Pottery Barn rule: If you break it, you fix it.

speaker: Moderator
text: Speaking of your plan, new question, Senator Kerry. Two minutes.

speaker: John Kerry
text: The time line that I’ve set out — and again, I want to correct the president, because he’s misled again this evening on what I’ve said. I didn’t say I would bring troops out in six months. I said, if we do the things that I’ve set out and we are successful, we could begin to draw the troops down in six months.

speaker: Moderator
text: Ninety seconds.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: There are 100,000 troops trained, police, guard, special units, border patrol. There’s going to be 125,000 trained by the end of this year. Yes, we’re getting the job done. It’s hard work. Everybody knows it’s hard work, because there’s a determined enemy that’s trying to defeat us.

speaker: Moderator
text: Thirty seconds.

speaker: John Kerry
text: I couldn’t agree more that the Iraqis want to be free and that they could be free.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Yes, let me…

speaker: Moderator
text: Yes, 30 seconds.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: The reason why Prime Minister Allawi said they’re coming across the border is because he recognizes that this is a central part of the war on terror. They’re fighting us because they’re fighting freedom.

speaker: Moderator
text: Mr. President, new question. Two minutes. Does the Iraq experience make it more likely or less likely that you would take the United States into another preemptive military action?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: I would hope I never have to. I understand how hard it is to commit troops. Never wanted to commit troops. When I was running — when we had the debate in 2000, never dreamt I’d be doing that.

speaker: Moderator
text: Senator Kerry, 90 seconds.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Jim, the president just said something extraordinarily revealing and frankly very important in this debate. In answer to your question about Iraq and sending people into Iraq, he just said, “The enemy attacked us.”

speaker: Moderator
text: Thirty seconds.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: First of all, of course I know Osama bin Laden attacked us. I know that.

speaker: Moderator
text: Thirty seconds, Senator.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Thirty-five to forty countries in the world had a greater capability of making weapons at the moment the president invaded than Saddam Hussein. And while he’s been diverted, with 9 out of 10 active duty divisions of our Army, either going to Iraq, coming back from Iraq, or getting ready to go, North Korea’s gotten nuclear weapons and the world is more dangerous. Iran is moving toward nuclear weapons and the world is more dangerous. Darfur has a genocide.

speaker: Moderator
text: New question. Two minutes, Senator Kerry.

speaker: Moderator
text: Ninety seconds.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Let me — I’m not exactly sure what you mean, “passes the global test,” you take preemptive action if you pass a global test.

speaker: Moderator
text: New question, Mr. President. Do you believe that diplomacy and sanctions can resolve the nuclear problems with North Korea and Iran? Take them in any order you would like.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: North Korea, first, I do. Let me say — I certainly hope so. Before I was sworn in, the policy of this government was to have bilateral negotiations with North Korea.

speaker: Moderator
text: Senator Kerry, 90 seconds.

speaker: John Kerry
text: With respect to Iran, the British, French, and Germans were the ones who initiated an effort without the United States, regrettably, to begin to try to move to curb the nuclear possibilities in Iran. I believe we could have done better. I think the United States should have offered the opportunity to provide the nuclear fuel, test them, see whether or not they were actually looking for it for peaceful purposes. If they weren’t willing to work a deal, then we could have put sanctions together. The president did nothing.

speaker: Moderator
text: I want to make sure — yes, sir — but in this one minute, I want to make sure that we understand — the people watching understand the differences between the two of you on this.

speaker: Moderator
text: And you’re willing to do it…

speaker: John Kerry
text: Both. I want bilateral talks which put all of the issues, from the armistice of 1952, the economic issues, the human rights issues, the artillery disposal issues, the DMZ issues and the nuclear issues on the table.

speaker: Moderator
text: And you’re opposed to that. Right?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: The minute we have bilateral talks, the six-party talks will unwind. That’s exactly what Kim Jong Il wants. And by the way, the breach on the agreement was not through plutonium. The breach on the agreement is highly enriched uranium. That’s what we caught him doing. That’s where he was breaking the agreement.

speaker: Moderator
text: New question, two minutes.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Well, I’ll tell you exactly why not, but I first want to say something about those sanctions on Iran.

speaker: Moderator
text: Ninety seconds.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Back to Iran, just for a second.

speaker: Moderator
text: New question, President Bush. Clearly, as we have heard, major policy differences between the two of you. Are there also underlying character issues that you believe, that you believe are serious enough to deny Senator Kerry the job as commander in chief of the United States?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: That’s a loaded question. Well, first of all, I admire Senator Kerry’s service to our country. I admire the fact that he is a great dad. I appreciate the fact that his daughters have been so kind to my daughters in what has been a pretty hard experience for, I guess, young girls, seeing their dads out there campaigning.

speaker: Moderator
text: Ninety second response, Senator.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Well, first of all, I appreciate enormously the personal comments the president just made. And I share them with him. I think only if you’re doing this — and he’s done it more than I have in terms of the presidency — can you begin to get a sense of what it means to your families. And it’s tough. And so I acknowledge that his daughters — I’ve watched them.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: I’m trying to put a leash on them.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Well, I know. I’ve learned not to do that.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Thank you.

speaker: John Kerry
text: … and a great first lady.

speaker: Moderator
text: Thirty seconds.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Well, I think — listen, I fully agree that one should shift tactics, and we will, in Iraq. Our commanders have got all the flexibility to do what is necessary to succeed.

speaker: Moderator
text: Thirty seconds.

speaker: John Kerry
text: I have no intention of wilting. I’ve never wilted in my life. And I’ve never wavered in my life.

speaker: Moderator
text: New question, two minutes, Senator Kerry.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Nuclear proliferation. Nuclear proliferation. There’s some 600-plus tons of unsecured material still in the former Soviet Union and Russia. At the rate that the president is currently securing it, it’ll take 13 years to get it.

speaker: Moderator
text: Ninety seconds, Mr. President.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Actually, we’ve increased funding for dealing with nuclear proliferation about 35 percent since I’ve been the president. Secondly, we’ve set up what’s called the — well, first of all, I agree with my opponent that the biggest threat facing this country is weapons of mass destruction in the hands of a terrorist network. And that’s why proliferation is one of the centerpieces of a multi-prong strategy to make the country safer.

speaker: Moderator
text: Just for this one-minute discussion here, just for whatever seconds it takes: So it’s correct to say, that if somebody is listening to this, that both of you agree, if you’re reelected, Mr. President, and if you are elected, the single most serious threat you believe, both of you believe, is nuclear proliferation?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: In the hands of a terrorist enemy.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Weapons of mass destruction, nuclear proliferation.

speaker: Moderator
text: Your response to that?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Again, I can’t tell you how big a mistake I think that is, to have bilateral talks with North Korea. It’s precisely what Kim Jong Il wants. It will cause the six-party talks to evaporate. It will mean that China no longer is involved in convincing, along with us, for Kim Jong Il to get rid of his weapons. It’s a big mistake to do that.

speaker: Moderator
text: All right. Mr. President, this is the last question. And two minutes. It’s a new subject — new question, and it has to do with President Putin and Russia. Did you misjudge him or are you — do you feel that what he is doing in the name of antiterrorism by changing some democratic processes is OK?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: No, I don’t think it’s OK, and said so publicly. I think that there needs to be checks and balances in a democracy, and made that very clear that by consolidating power in the central government, he’s sending a signal to the Western world and United States that perhaps he doesn’t believe in checks and balances, and I told him that.

speaker: Moderator
text: Ninety seconds, Senator Kerry.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Well, let me just say quickly that I’ve had an extraordinary experience of watching up close and personal that transition in Russia, because I was there right after the transformation. And I was probably one of the first senators, along with Senator Bob Smith of New Hampshire, a former senator, to go down into the KGB underneath Treblinka Square and see reams of files with names in them.

speaker: Moderator
text: Thirty seconds, Mr. President.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: You know my opinion on North Korea. I can’t say it any more plainly.

speaker: Moderator
text: Well, but when he used the word “truth” again…

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Pardon me?

speaker: Moderator
text: … talking about the truth of the matter. He used the word “truth” again. Did that raise any hackles with you?

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Oh, I’m a pretty calm guy. I don’t take it personally.

speaker: Moderator
text: OK. All right.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: You know, we looked at the same intelligence and came to the same conclusion: that Saddam Hussein was a grave threat.

speaker: John Kerry
text: It was a threat. That’s not the issue. The issue is what you do about it.

speaker: Moderator
text: All right, that brings us to closing statements.

speaker: John Kerry
text: Thank you, Jim, very much.

speaker: Moderator
text: Mr. President, two minutes.

speaker: George H.W. Bush
text: Thank you very much tonight, Jim. Senator.

speaker: Moderator
text: And that ends tonight’s debate. A reminder, the second presidential debate will be a week from tomorrow, October 8th, from Washington University in St. Louis. Charles Gibson of ABC News will moderate a town hall-type event. Then, on October 13th, from Arizona State University in Tempe, Bob Schieffer of CBS News will moderate an exchange on domestic policy that will be similar in format to tonight’s.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, let — let me say, Bob, thank you.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, what about the citizen that stayed in their homes? That paid their mortgage payments? It doesn’t help that person in their home if the next door neighbor’s house is abandoned. And so we’ve got to reverse this. We ought to put the homeowners first. And I am disappointed that Secretary Paulson and others have not made that their first priority.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right. Senator Obama?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, first of all, I want to thank Hofstra University and the people of New York for hosting us tonight and it’s wonderful to join Senator McCain again, and thank you, Bob.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right. Would you like to ask him a question?

speaker: John McCain
text: No. I would like to mention that a couple days ago Senator Obama was out in Ohio and he had an encounter with a guy who’s a plumber, his name is Joe Wurzelbacher.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Is that what you want to do?

speaker: John McCain
text: That’s what Joe believes.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: He has been watching ads of Senator McCain’s. Let me tell you what I’m actually going to do. I think tax policy is a major difference between Senator McCain and myself. And we both want to cut taxes, the difference is who we want to cut taxes for.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Now, the conversation I had with Joe the plumber, what I essentially said to him was, “Five years ago, when you were in a position to buy your business, you needed a tax cut then.”

speaker: John McCain
text: You know, when Senator Obama ended up his conversation with Joe the plumber — we need to spread the wealth around. In other words, we’re going to take Joe’s money, give it to Senator Obama, and let him spread the wealth around.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: OK. Can I…

speaker: John McCain
text: We’re not going to do that in my administration.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: If I can answer the question. Number one, I want to cut taxes for 95 percent of Americans. Now, it is true that my friend and supporter, Warren Buffett, for example, could afford to pay a little more in taxes in order…

speaker: John McCain
text: We’re talking about Joe the plumber. OBAMA: … in order to give — in order to give additional tax cuts to Joe the plumber before he was at the point where he could make $250,000.

speaker: John McCain
text: Nobody likes taxes. Let’s not raise anybody’s taxes. OK?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, I don’t mind paying a little more.

speaker: John McCain
text: The fact is that businesses in America today are paying the second highest tax rate of anywhere in the world. Our tax rate for business in America is 35 percent. Ireland, it’s 11 percent.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right. Let’s go to another topic. It’s related. So if you have other things you want to say, you can get back to that.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, first of all, I think it’s important for the American public to understand that the $750 billion rescue package, if it’s structured properly, and, as president, I will make sure it’s structured properly, means that ultimately taxpayers get their money back, and that’s important to understand.

speaker: Schieffer
text: But you’re going to have to cut some of these programs, certainly.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Absolutely. So let me get to that. What I want to emphasize, though, is that I have been a strong proponent of pay-as- you-go. Every dollar that I’ve proposed, I’ve proposed an additional cut so that it matches.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: And some of the cuts, just to give you an example, we spend $15 billion a year on subsidies to insurance companies. It doesn’t — under the Medicare plan — it doesn’t help seniors get any better. It’s not improving our health care system. It’s just a giveaway.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Time’s up.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, thank you, Bob. I just want to get back to this home ownership. During the Depression era, we had a thing called the home ownership loan corporation.

speaker: John McCain
text: But — OK. All right.

speaker: Schieffer
text: The question was, what are you going to cut?

speaker: John McCain
text: Energy — well, first — second of all, energy independence. We have to have nuclear power. We have to stop sending $700 billion a year to countries that don’t like us very much. It’s wind, tide, solar, natural gas, nuclear, off-shore drilling, which Senator Obama has opposed.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Which ones?

speaker: John McCain
text: I have fought against — well, one of them would be the marketing assistance program. Another one would be a number of subsidies for ethanol.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Time’s up.

speaker: John McCain
text: … including $3 million for an overhead projector in a planetarium in his hometown. That’s not the way we cut — we’ll cut out all the pork.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Time’s up.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, look, I think that we do have a disagreement about an across-the-board spending freeze. It sounds good. It’s proposed periodically. It doesn’t happen.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: And we are now looking at a deficit of well over half a trillion dollars.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Do either of you think you can balance the budget in four years? You have said previously you thought you could, Senator McCain.

speaker: John McCain
text: Sure I do. And let me tell you…

speaker: Schieffer
text: You can still do that?

speaker: John McCain
text: Yes. Senator Obama, I am not President Bush. If you wanted to run against President Bush, you should have run four years ago. I’m going to give a new direction to this economy in this country.

speaker: Schieffer
text: In four years?

speaker: John McCain
text: … reduce this — I can — we can do it with this kind of job creation of energy independence.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, there’s a lot of stuff that was put out there, so let me try to address it. First of all, in terms of standing up to the leaders of my party, the first major bill that I voted on in the Senate was in support of tort reform, which wasn’t very popular with trial lawyers, a major constituency in the Democratic Party. I support…

speaker: John McCain
text: An overwhelming vote.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I support charter schools and pay for performance for teachers. Doesn’t make me popular with the teachers union. I support clean coal technology. Doesn’t make me popular with environmentalists. So I’ve got a history of reaching across the aisle.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right…

speaker: John McCain
text: Let me just say, Bob.

speaker: Schieffer
text: OK. About 30 seconds.

speaker: John McCain
text: OK. But it’s very clear that I have disagreed with the Bush administration. I have disagreed with leaders of my own party. I’ve got the scars to prove it.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right.

speaker: John McCain
text: Senator Obama, your argument for standing up to the leadership of your party isn’t very convincing.

speaker: Schieffer
text: All right. We’re going to move to another question and the topic is leadership in this campaign. Both of you pledged to take the high road in this campaign yet it has turned very nasty.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Senator Obama, your campaign has used words like “erratic,” “out of touch,” “lie,” “angry,” “losing his bearings” to describe Senator McCain.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, this has been a tough campaign. It’s been a very tough campaign. And I know from my experience in many campaigns that, if Senator Obama had asked — responded to my urgent request to sit down, and do town hall meetings, and come before the American people, we could have done at least 10 of them by now.

speaker: Schieffer
text: Time’s up. All right.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, look, you know, I think that we expect presidential campaigns to be tough. I think that, if you look at the record and the impressions of the American people — Bob, your network just did a poll, showing that two-thirds of the American people think that Senator McCain is running a negative campaign versus one-third of mine.

speaker: John McCain
text: It’s not true.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: It absolutely is true. And, now, I think the American people are less interested in our hurt feelings during the course of the campaign than addressing the issues that matter to them so deeply.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, if you’ll turn on the television, as I — I watched the Arizona Cardinals defeat the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Congratulations.

speaker: John McCain
text: Every other ad — ever other ad was an attack ad on my health care plan. And any objective observer has said it’s not true. You’re running ads right now that say that I oppose federal funding for stem cell research. I don’t.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I mean, look, if we want to talk about Congressman Lewis, who is an American hero, he, unprompted by my campaign, without my campaign’s awareness, made a statement that he was troubled with what he was hearing at some of the rallies that your running mate was holding, in which all the Republican reports indicated were shouting, when my name came up, things like “terrorist” and “kill him,” and that you’re running mate didn’t mention, didn’t stop, didn’t say “Hold on a second, that’s kind of out of line.”

speaker: John McCain
text: You’ve got to read what he said…

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Let — let — let… MCCAIN: You’ve got to read what he said.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Let me — let me complete…

speaker: Barack Obama
text: … my response. I do think that he inappropriately drew a comparison between what was happening there and what had happened during the civil rights movement, and we immediately put out a statement saying that we don’t think that comparison is appropriate.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: We can have serious differences about our health care policy, for example, John, because we do have a difference on health care policy, but we…

speaker: John McCain
text: We do and I hope…

speaker: Barack Obama
