text: That’s not true, John. That’s not true.

speaker: John McCain
text: And that’s just a fact. Again, you can look it up.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Look, it’s just not true. And if we want to talk about oil company profits, under your tax plan, John — this is undeniable — oil companies would get an additional $4 billion in tax breaks.

speaker: John McCain
text: With all due respect, you already gave them to the oil companies.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: No, but, John, the fact of the matter is, is that I was opposed to those tax breaks, tried to strip them out. We’ve got an energy bill on the Senate floor right now that contains some good stuff, some stuff you want, including drilling off-shore, but you’re opposed to it because it would strip away those tax breaks that have gone to oil companies.

speaker: Moderator
text: All right. All right, speaking of things that both of you want, another lead question, and it has to do with the rescue — the financial rescue thing that we started — started asking about.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, there are a range of things that are probably going to have to be delayed. We don’t yet know what our tax revenues are going to be. The economy is slowing down, so it’s hard to anticipate right now what the budget is going to look like next year.

speaker: Moderator
text: Are you — what priorities would you adjust, as president, Senator McCain, because of the — because of the financial bailout cost?

speaker: John McCain
text: Look, we, no matter what, we’ve got to cut spending. We have — as I said, we’ve let government get completely out of control.

speaker: John McCain
text: I saved the taxpayers $6.8 billion by fighting a contract that was negotiated between Boeing and DOD that was completely wrong. And we fixed it and we killed it and the people ended up in federal prison so I know how to do this because I’ve been involved these issues for many, many years. But I think that we have to examine every agency of government and find out those that are doing their job and keep them and find out those that aren’t and eliminate them and we’ll have to scrub every agency of government.

speaker: Moderator
text: But if I hear the two of you correctly neither one of you is suggesting any major changes in what you want to do as president as a result of the financial bailout? Is that what you’re saying?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: No. As I said before, Jim, there are going to be things that end up having to be …

speaker: Moderator
text: Like what?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: … deferred and delayed. Well, look, I want to make sure that we are investing in energy in order to free ourselves from the dependence on foreign oil. That is a big project. That is a multi-year project.

speaker: Moderator
text: Not willing to give that up?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Not willing to give up the need to do it but there may be individual components that we can’t do. But John is right we have to make cuts. We right now give $15 billion every year as subsidies to private insurers under the Medicare system. Doesn’t work any better through the private insurers. They just skim off $15 billion. That was a give away and part of the reason is because lobbyists are able to shape how Medicare works.

speaker: Moderator
text: What I’m trying to get at this is this. Excuse me if I may, senator. Trying to get at that you all — one of you is going to be the president of the United States come January. At the — in the middle of a huge financial crisis that is yet to be resolved. And what I’m trying to get at is how this is going to affect you not in very specific — small ways but in major ways and the approach to take as to the presidency.

speaker: John McCain
text: How about a spending freeze on everything but defense, veteran affairs and entitlement programs.

speaker: Moderator
text: Spending freeze?

speaker: John McCain
text: I think we ought to seriously consider with the exceptions of caring for our veterans national defense and several other vital issues.

speaker: Moderator
text: Would you go for that?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: The problem with a spending freeze is you’re using a hatchet where you need a scalpel. There are some programs that are very important that are under funded. I went to increase early childhood education and the notion that we should freeze that when there may be, for example, this Medicare subsidy, I think, doesn’t make sense.

speaker: John McCain
text: Look, we are sending $700 billion a year overseas to countries that don’t like us very much. Some of that money ends up in the hands of terrorist organizations. We have to have wind, tide, solar, natural gas, flex fuel cars and all that but we also have to have offshore drilling and we also have to have nuclear power.

speaker: Moderator
text: Before we go to another lead question. Let me figure out a way to ask the same question in a slightly different way here. Are you — are you willing to acknowledge both of you that this financial crisis is going to affect the way you rule the country as president of the United States beyond the kinds of things that you have already — I mean, is it a major move? Is it going to have a major affect?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: There’s no doubt itâ€™s gonna affect our budgets. There is no doubt about it. Not only — Even if we get all $700 billion back, let’s assume the markets recover, we’re holding assets long enough that eventually taxpayers get it back and that happened during the Great Depression when Roosevelt purchased a whole bunch of homes, over time, home values went back up and in fact government made a profit. If we’re lucky and we do it right, that could potentially happen but in the short term there’s an outlay and we may not see that money for a while.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, I want to make sure we’re not handing the health care system over to the federal government which is basically what would ultimately happen with Senator Obama’s health care plan. I want the families to make decisions between themselves and their doctors. Not the federal government. Look. We have to obviously cut spending. I have fought to cut spending. Senator Obama has $800 billion in new spending programs. I would suggest he start by canceling some of those new spending program that he has.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I just want to make this point, Jim. John, it’s been your president who you said you agreed with 90 percent of the time who presided over this increase in spending. This orgy of spending and enormous deficits you voted for almost all of his budgets. So to stand here and after eight years and say that you’re going to lead on controlling spending and, you know, balancing our tax cuts so that they help middle class families when over the last eight years that hasn’t happened I think just is, you know, kind of hard to swallow.

speaker: Moderator
text: Quick response to Senator Obama.

speaker: John McCain
text: It’s well-known that I have not been elected Miss Congeniality in the United States Senate nor with the administration. I have opposed the president on spending, on climate change, on torture of prisoner, on – on Guantanamo Bay. On a — on the way that the Iraq War was conducted. I have a long record and the American people know me very well and that is independent and a maverick of the Senate and I’m happy to say that I’ve got a partner that’s a good maverick along with me now.

speaker: Moderator
text: All right. Let’s go another subject. Lead question, two minutes to you, senator McCain. Much has been said about the lessons of Vietnam. What do you see as the lessons of Iraq?

speaker: John McCain
text: I think the lessons of Iraq are very clear that you cannot have a failed strategy that will then cause you to nearly lose a conflict. Our initial military success, we went in to Baghdad and everybody celebrated. And then the war was very badly mishandled. I went to Iraq in 2003 and came back and said, we’ve got to change this strategy. This strategy requires additional troops, it requires a fundamental change in strategy and I fought for it. And finally, we came up with a great general and a strategy that has succeeded.

speaker: John McCain
text: And I want to tell you that now that we will succeed and our troops will come home, and not in defeat, that we will see a stable ally in the region and a fledgling democracy.

speaker: Moderator
text: Two minutes, how you see the lessons of Iraq, Senator Obama.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, this is an area where Senator McCain and I have a fundamental difference because I think the first question is whether we should have gone into the war in the first place.

speaker: Moderator
text: Do you agree with that, the lesson of Iraq?

speaker: John McCain
text: The next president of the United States is not going to have to address the issue as to whether we went into Iraq or not. The next president of the United States is going to have to decide how we leave, when we leave, and what we leave behind. That’s the decision of the next president of the United States.

speaker: Moderator
text: Well, let’s go at some of these things…

speaker: John McCain
text: Senator Obama is the chairperson of a committee that oversights NATO that’s in Afghanistan. To this day, he has never had a hearing.

speaker: Moderator
text: What about that point?

speaker: John McCain
text: I mean, it’s remarkable.

speaker: Moderator
text: All right. What about that point?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Which point? He raised a whole bunch of them.

speaker: Moderator
text: I know, OK, let’s go to the latter point and we’ll back up. The point about your not having been…

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Look, I’m very proud of my vice presidential selection, Joe Biden, who is the chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and as he explains, and as John well knows, the issues of Afghanistan, the issues of Iraq, critical issues like that, don’t go through my subcommittee because they’re done as a committee as a whole.

speaker: Moderator
text: Senator Obama…

speaker: Barack Obama
text: … of judgment, of whether or not — of whether or not — if the question is who is best-equipped as the next president to make good decisions about how we use our military, how we make sure that we are prepared and ready for the next conflict, then I think we can take a look at our judgment.

speaker: Moderator
text: I have got a lot on the plate here…

speaker: John McCain
text: I’m afraid Senator Obama doesn’t understand the difference between a tactic and a strategy. But the important — I’d like to tell you, two Fourths of July ago I was in Baghdad. General Petraeus invited Senator Lindsey Graham and me to attend a ceremony where 688 brave young Americans, whose enlistment had expired, were reenlisting to stay and fight for Iraqi freedom and American freedom.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: That’s not true.

speaker: John McCain
text: They just passed an electoral…

speaker: Barack Obama
text: That’s not true.

speaker: John McCain
text: An election law just in the last few days. There is social, economic progress, and a strategy, a strategy of going into an area, clearing and holding, and the people of the country then become allied with you. They inform on the bad guys. And peace comes to the country, and prosperity.

speaker: Moderator
text: Let me see…

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Jim, Jim, this is a big…

speaker: John McCain
text: It was a strategy. And that same strategy will be employed in Afghanistan by this great general. And Senator Obama, who after promising not to vote to cut off funds for the troops, did the incredible thing of voting to cut off the funds for the troops in Iraq and Afghanistan.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Jim, there are a whole bunch of things we have got to answer. First of all, let’s talk about this troop funding issue because John always brings this up. Senator McCain cut — Senator McCain opposed funding for troops in legislation that had a timetable, because he didn’t believe in a timetable.

speaker: John McCain
text: Admiral Mullen suggests that Senator Obama’s plan is dangerous for America.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: That’s not the case.

speaker: John McCain
text: That’s what …

speaker: Barack Obama
text: What he said was a precipitous…

speaker: John McCain
text: That’s what Admiral Mullen said.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: … withdrawal would be dangerous. He did not say that. That’s not true.

speaker: John McCain
text: And also General Petraeus said the same thing. Osama bin Laden and General Petraeus have one thing in common that I know of, they both said that Iraq is the central battleground.

speaker: John McCain
text: It didn’t exceed beyond mine, because I know that that’s a strategy that has worked and can succeed. But if we snatch defeat from the jaws of victory and adopt Senator Obama’s plan, then we will have a wider war and it will make things more complicated throughout the region, including in Afghanistan.

speaker: Moderator
text: Afghanistan, lead — a new — a new lead question. Now, having resolved Iraq, we’ll move to Afghanistan.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Yes, I think we need more troops. I’ve been saying that for over a year now.

speaker: Moderator
text: Afghanistan, Senator McCain?

speaker: John McCain
text: First of all, I won’t repeat the mistake that I regret enormously, and that is, after we were able to help the Afghan freedom fighters and drive the Russians out of Afghanistan, we basically washed our hands of the region.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Nobody talked about attacking Pakistan. Here’s what I said.

speaker: John McCain
text: I — I don’t think that Senator Obama understands that there was a failed state in Pakistan when Musharraf came to power. Everybody who was around then, and had been there, and knew about it knew that it was a failed state.

speaker: John McCain
text: A war that I was in, where we had an Army, that it wasn’t through any fault of their own, but they were defeated. And I know how hard it is for that — for an Army and a military to recover from that. And it did and we will win this one and we won’t come home in defeat and dishonor and probably have to go back if we fail.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Jim, let me just make a point. I’ve got a bracelet, too, from Sergeant – from the mother of Sergeant Ryan David Jopeck (ph), given to me in green bay. She asked me, can you please make sure another mother is not going through what I’m going through.

speaker: John McCain
text: You might think that with that kind of concern that Senator Obama would have gone to Afghanistan, particularly given his responsibilities as a subcommittee chairman. By the way, when I’m subcommittee chairman, we take up the issues under my subcommittee. But the important thing is — the important thing is I visited Afghanistan and I traveled to Waziristan and I traveled to these places and I know what our security requirements are. I know what our needs are. So the point is that we will prevail in Afghanistan, but we need the new strategy and we need it to succeed.

speaker: Moderator
text: I have some good news and bad news for the two of you. You all are even on time, which is remarkable, considering we’ve been going at it …

speaker: Barack Obama
text: A testimony to you, Jim.

speaker: Moderator
text: I don’t know about that. But the bad news is all my little five minute things have run over, so, anyhow, we’ll adjust as we get there. But the amount of time is even.

speaker: John McCain
text: My reading of the threat from Iran is that if Iran acquires nuclear weapons, it is an existential threat to the State of Israel and it is a threat to other countries in the region because the other countries in the region will feel compelling requirement to acquire nuclear weapons as well.

speaker: Moderator
text: Two minutes on Iran, Senator Obama.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, let me just correct something very quickly. I believe the Republican Guard of Iran is a terrorist organization. I’ve consistently said so. What Senator McCain refers to is a measure in the Senate that would try to broaden the mandate inside of Iraq. To deal with Iran.

speaker: Moderator
text: Senator, what about talking?

speaker: John McCain
text: Senator Obama twice said in debates he would sit down with Ahmadinejad, Chavez and Raul Castro without precondition. Without precondition. Here is Ahmadinenene (ph), Ahmadinejad, who is, Ahmadinejad, who is now in New York, talking about the extermination of the State of Israel, of wiping Israel off the map, and we’re going to sit down, without precondition, across the table, to legitimize and give a propaganda platform to a person that is espousing the extermination of the state of Israel, and therefore then giving them more credence in the world arena and therefore saying, they’ve probably been doing the right thing, because you will sit down across the table from them and that will legitimize their illegal behavior.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: So let’s talk about this. First of all, Ahmadinejad is not the most powerful person in Iran. So he may not be the right person to talk to. But I reserve the right, as president of the United States to meet with anybody at a time and place of my choosing if I think it’s going to keep America safe.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Senator McCain mentioned Henry Kissinger, who’s one of his advisers, who, along with five recent secretaries of state, just said that we should meet with Iran — guess what — without precondition. This is one of your own advisers.

speaker: John McCain
text: Of course.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: If we can’t meet with our friends, I don’t know how we’re going to lead the world in terms of dealing with critical issues like terrorism.

speaker: John McCain
text: I’m not going to set the White House visitors schedule before I’m president of the United States. I don’t even have a seal yet.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Of course not.

speaker: John McCain
text: He said that there could be secretary-level and lower level meetings. I’ve always encouraged them. The Iranians have met with Ambassador Crocker in Baghdad.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Look, I mean, Senator McCain keeps on using this example that suddenly the president would just meet with somebody without doing any preparation, without having low-level talks. Nobody’s been talking about that, and Senator McCain knows it. This is a mischaracterization of my position.

speaker: John McCain
text: So let me get this right. We sit down with Ahmadinejad, and he says, “We’re going to wipe Israel off the face of the Earth,” and we say, “No, you’re not”? Oh, please.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: No, let me tell…

speaker: John McCain
text: By the way, my friend, Dr. Kissinger, who’s been my friend for 35 years, would be interested to hear this conversation and Senator Obama’s depiction of his — of his positions on the issue. I’ve known him for 35 years.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: We will take a look.

speaker: John McCain
text: And I guarantee you he would not — he would not say that presidential top level.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Nobody’s talking about that.

speaker: John McCain
text: Of course he encourages and other people encourage contacts, and negotiations, and all other things. We do that all the time.

speaker: Moderator
text: We’re going to go to a new…

speaker: John McCain
text: And Senator Obama is parsing words when he says precondition means preparation.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I am not parsing words.

speaker: John McCain
text: He’s parsing words, my friends.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I’m using the same words that your advisers use.

speaker: Moderator
text: New lead question.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, I think that, given what’s happened over the last several weeks and months, our entire Russian approach has to be evaluated, because a resurgent and very aggressive Russia is a threat to the peace and stability of the region.

speaker: Moderator
text: Two minutes on Russia, Senator McCain.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, I was interested in Senator Obama’s reaction to the Russian aggression against Georgia. His first statement was, “Both sides ought to show restraint.”

speaker: John McCain
text: And they showed solidarity with them, but, also, they are very concerned about the Russian threats to regain their status of the old Russian to regain their status of the old Russian empire.

speaker: Moderator
text: You see any — do you have a major difference with what he just said?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: No, actually, I think Senator McCain and I agree for the most part on these issues. Obviously, I disagree with this notion that somehow we did not forcefully object to Russians going into Georgia.

speaker: Moderator
text: We’ve got time for one more lead question segment. We’re way out of…

speaker: Moderator
text: Quick response and then…

speaker: John McCain
text: No one from Arizona is against solar. And Senator Obama says he’s for nuclear, but he’s against reprocessing and he’s against storing. So…

speaker: Barack Obama
text: That’s just not true, John. John, I’m sorry, but that’s not true.

speaker: John McCain
text: … it’s hard to get there from here. And off-shore drilling is also something that is very important and it is a bridge.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I just have to respond very quickly, just to correct — just to correct the record.

speaker: John McCain
text: So I want to say that, with the Nunn-Lugar thing…

speaker: Moderator
text: Excuse me, Senator.

speaker: John McCain
text: … I supported Nunn-Lugar back in the early 1990s when a lot of my colleagues didn’t. That was the key legislation at the time and put us on the road to eliminating this issue of nuclear waste and the nuclear fuel that has to be taken care of.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I — I just have to correct the record here. I have never said that I object to nuclear waste. What I’ve said is that we have to store it safely.

speaker: Moderator
text: All right.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I’ve got to make this point, Jim.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: He objects…

speaker: John McCain
text: I have voted for alternate fuel all of my time…

speaker: Barack Obama
text: He — he — he objects…

speaker: Moderator
text: One at a time, please.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: He objected…

speaker: Moderator
text: One at a time.

speaker: John McCain
text: No one can be opposed to alternate energy.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: All right, fair enough. Let’s move on. You’ve got one more energy — you’ve got one more question.

speaker: Moderator
text: This is the last — last lead question. You have two minutes each. And the question is this, beginning with you, Senator McCain.

speaker: John McCain
text: I think it’s much less than it was the day after 9/11. I think it — that we have a safer nation, but we are a long way from safe.

speaker: Moderator
text: Two minutes, Senator Obama.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, first of all, I think that we are safer in some ways. Obviously, we’ve poured billions of dollars into airport security. We have done some work in terms of securing potential targets, but we still have a long way to go.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: And this is the greatest country on Earth. But because of some of the mistakes that have been made — and I give Senator McCain great credit on the torture issue, for having identified that as something that undermines our long-term security — because of those things, we, I think, are going to have a lot of work to do in the next administration to restore that sense that America is that shining beacon on a hill.

speaker: Moderator
text: Do you agree there’s much to be done in a new administration to restore…

speaker: John McCain
text: But in the case of missile defense, Senator Obama said it had to be, quote, “proven.” That wasn’t proven when Ronald Reagan said we would do SDI, which is missile defense. And it was major — a major factor in bringing about the end of the Cold War.

speaker: Moderator
text: You see the same connections that Senator McCain does?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Oh, there’s no doubt. Look, over the last eight years, this administration, along with Senator McCain, have been solely focused on Iraq. That has been their priority. That has been where all our resources have gone.

speaker: John McCain
text: I’ve been involved, as I mentioned to you before, in virtually every major national security challenge we’ve faced in the last 20-some years. There are some advantages to experience, and knowledge, and judgment.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, let me just make a closing point. You know, my father came from Kenya. That’s where I get my name.

speaker: Moderator
text: Few seconds. We’re almost finished.

speaker: John McCain
text: Jim, when I came home from prison, I saw our veterans being very badly treated, and it made me sad. And I embarked on an effort to resolve the POW-MIA issue, which we did in a bipartisan fashion, and then I worked on normalization of relations between our two countries so that our veterans could come all the way home.

speaker: Moderator
text: And that ends this debate tonight.

speaker: Gerald Ford
text: U.S. SENATOR JOHN MCCAIN (AZ)

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, thank you very much, Jim, and thanks to the commission and the University of Mississippi, Ole Miss, for hosting us tonight. I can’t think of a more important time for us to talk about the future of the country.

speaker: Moderator
text: Senator McCain, two minutes.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, thank you, Jim. And thanks to everybody.

speaker: Moderator
text: All right, let’s go back to my question. How do you all stand on the recovery plan? And talk to each other about it. We’ve got five minutes. We can negotiate a deal right here.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: We haven’t seen the language yet. And I do think that there’s constructive work being done out there. So, for the viewers who are watching, I am optimistic about the capacity of us to come together with a plan.

speaker: Moderator
text: Are you going to vote for the plan, Senator McCain?

speaker: John McCain
text: I — I hope so. And I…

speaker: Moderator
text: As a United States senator…

speaker: Moderator
text: … you’re going to vote for the plan?

speaker: John McCain
text: Sure. But — but let me — let me point out, I also warned about Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and warned about corporate greed and excess, and CEO pay, and all that. A lot of us saw this train wreck coming.

speaker: Moderator
text: Do you have something directly to say, Senator Obama, to Senator McCain about what he just said?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, I think Senator McCain’s absolutely right that we need more responsibility, but we need it not just when there’s a crisis. I mean, we’ve had years in which the reigning economic ideology has been what’s good for Wall Street, but not what’s good for Main Street.

speaker: Moderator
text: Say it directly to him.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I do not think that they are.

speaker: Moderator
text: Say it directly to him.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, the — John, 10 days ago, you said that the fundamentals of the economy are sound. And…

speaker: John McCain
text: Are you afraid I couldn’t hear him?

speaker: Moderator
text: I’m just determined to get you all to talk to each other. I’m going to try.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: The — and I just fundamentally disagree. And unless we are holding ourselves accountable day in, day out, not just when there’s a crisis for folks who have power and influence and can hire lobbyists, but for the nurse, the teacher, the police officer, who, frankly, at the end of each month, they’ve got a little financial crisis going on.

speaker: Moderator
text: So, Senator McCain, do you agree with what Senator Obama just said? And, if you don’t, tell him what you disagree with.

speaker: John McCain
text: No, I — look, we’ve got to fix the system. We’ve got fundamental problems in the system. And Main Street is paying a penalty for the excesses and greed in Washington, D.C., and in the Wall Street.

speaker: Moderator
text: All right, let’s go to the next lead question, which is essentially following up on this same subject.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, the first thing we have to do is get spending under control in Washington. It’s completely out of control. It’s gone — we have now presided over the largest increase in the size of government since the Great Society.

speaker: Moderator
text: Senator Obama, two minutes.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, Senator McCain is absolutely right that the earmarks process has been abused, which is why I suspended any requests for my home state, whether it was for senior centers or what have you, until we cleaned it up.

speaker: Moderator
text: Senator McCain?

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, again, I don’t mean to go back and forth, but he…

speaker: Moderator
text: No, that’s fine.

speaker: John McCain
text: Senator Obama suspended those requests for pork-barrel projects after he was running for president of the United States. He didn’t happen to see that light during the first three years as a member of the United States Senate, $932 million in requests.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I — I don’t know where John is getting his figures. Let’s just be clear.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: And when you look at your tax policies that are directed primarily at those who are doing well, and you are neglecting people who are really struggling right now, I think that is a continuation of the last eight years, and we can’t afford another four.

speaker: Moderator
text: Respond directly to him about that, to Senator Obama about that, about the — he’s made it twice now, about your tax — your policies about tax cuts.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well — well, let me give you an example of what Senator Obama finds objectionable, the business tax.

speaker: Moderator
text: Senator Obama, you have a question for Senator McCain on that?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, let me just make a couple of points.

speaker: Moderator
text: All right.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: My definition — here’s what I can tell the American people: 95 percent of you will get a tax cut. And if you make less than $250,000, less than a quarter-million dollars a year, then you will not see one dime’s worth of tax increase.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, you know, let me just…

speaker: Moderator
text: We’ve got to go to another lead question.

speaker: John McCain
text: I know we have to, but this is a classic example of walking the walk and talking the talk.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: John, you want to give oil companies another $4 billion.

speaker: John McCain
text: You’ve got to look at our record. You’ve got to look at our records. That’s the important thing.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: That’s not true, John. That’s not true.

speaker: John McCain
text: And that’s just a fact. Again, you can look it up.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Look, it’s just not true. And if we want to talk about oil company profits, under your tax plan, John — this is undeniable — oil companies would get an additional $4 billion in tax breaks.

speaker: John McCain
text: With all due respect, you already gave them to the oil companies.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: No, but, John, the fact of the matter is, is that I was opposed to those tax breaks, tried to strip them out. We’ve got an energy bill on the Senate floor right now that contains some good stuff, some stuff you want, including drilling off-shore, but you’re opposed to it because it would strip away those tax breaks that have gone to oil companies.

speaker: Moderator
text: All right. All right, speaking of things that both of you want, another lead question, and it has to do with the rescue — the financial rescue thing that we started — started asking about.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, there are a range of things that are probably going to have to be delayed. We don’t yet know what our tax revenues are going to be. The economy is slowing down, so it’s hard to anticipate right now what the budget is going to look like next year.

speaker: Moderator
text: Are you — what priorities would you adjust, as president, Senator McCain, because of the — because of the financial bailout cost?

speaker: John McCain
text: Look, we, no matter what, we’ve got to cut spending. We have — as I said, we’ve let government get completely out of control.

speaker: John McCain
text: I saved the taxpayers $6.8 billion by fighting a contract that was negotiated between Boeing and DOD that was completely wrong. And we fixed it and we killed it and the people ended up in federal prison so I know how to do this because I’ve been involved these issues for many, many years. But I think that we have to examine every agency of government and find out those that are doing their job and keep them and find out those that aren’t and eliminate them and we’ll have to scrub every agency of government.

speaker: Moderator
text: But if I hear the two of you correctly neither one of you is suggesting any major changes in what you want to do as president as a result of the financial bailout? Is that what you’re saying?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: No. As I said before, Jim, there are going to be things that end up having to be …

speaker: Moderator
text: Like what?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: … deferred and delayed. Well, look, I want to make sure that we are investing in energy in order to free ourselves from the dependence on foreign oil. That is a big project. That is a multi-year project.

speaker: Moderator
text: Not willing to give that up?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Not willing to give up the need to do it but there may be individual components that we can’t do. But John is right we have to make cuts. We right now give $15 billion every year as subsidies to private insurers under the Medicare system. Doesn’t work any better through the private insurers. They just skim off $15 billion. That was a give away and part of the reason is because lobbyists are able to shape how Medicare works.

speaker: Moderator
text: What I’m trying to get at this is this. Excuse me if I may, senator. Trying to get at that you all — one of you is going to be the president of the United States come January. At the — in the middle of a huge financial crisis that is yet to be resolved. And what I’m trying to get at is how this is going to affect you not in very specific — small ways but in major ways and the approach to take as to the presidency.

speaker: John McCain
text: How about a spending freeze on everything but defense, veteran affairs and entitlement programs.

speaker: Moderator
text: Spending freeze?

speaker: John McCain
text: I think we ought to seriously consider with the exceptions of caring for our veterans national defense and several other vital issues.

speaker: Moderator
text: Would you go for that?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: The problem with a spending freeze is you’re using a hatchet where you need a scalpel. There are some programs that are very important that are under funded. I went to increase early childhood education and the notion that we should freeze that when there may be, for example, this Medicare subsidy, I think, doesn’t make sense.

speaker: John McCain
text: Look, we are sending $700 billion a year overseas to countries that don’t like us very much. Some of that money ends up in the hands of terrorist organizations. We have to have wind, tide, solar, natural gas, flex fuel cars and all that but we also have to have offshore drilling and we also have to have nuclear power.

speaker: Moderator
text: Before we go to another lead question. Let me figure out a way to ask the same question in a slightly different way here. Are you — are you willing to acknowledge both of you that this financial crisis is going to affect the way you rule the country as president of the United States beyond the kinds of things that you have already — I mean, is it a major move? Is it going to have a major affect?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: There’s no doubt itâ€™s gonna affect our budgets. There is no doubt about it. Not only — Even if we get all $700 billion back, let’s assume the markets recover, we’re holding assets long enough that eventually taxpayers get it back and that happened during the Great Depression when Roosevelt purchased a whole bunch of homes, over time, home values went back up and in fact government made a profit. If we’re lucky and we do it right, that could potentially happen but in the short term there’s an outlay and we may not see that money for a while.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, I want to make sure we’re not handing the health care system over to the federal government which is basically what would ultimately happen with Senator Obama’s health care plan. I want the families to make decisions between themselves and their doctors. Not the federal government. Look. We have to obviously cut spending. I have fought to cut spending. Senator Obama has $800 billion in new spending programs. I would suggest he start by canceling some of those new spending program that he has.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I just want to make this point, Jim. John, it’s been your president who you said you agreed with 90 percent of the time who presided over this increase in spending. This orgy of spending and enormous deficits you voted for almost all of his budgets. So to stand here and after eight years and say that you’re going to lead on controlling spending and, you know, balancing our tax cuts so that they help middle class families when over the last eight years that hasn’t happened I think just is, you know, kind of hard to swallow.

speaker: Moderator
text: Quick response to Senator Obama.

speaker: John McCain
text: It’s well-known that I have not been elected Miss Congeniality in the United States Senate nor with the administration. I have opposed the president on spending, on climate change, on torture of prisoner, on – on Guantanamo Bay. On a — on the way that the Iraq War was conducted. I have a long record and the American people know me very well and that is independent and a maverick of the Senate and I’m happy to say that I’ve got a partner that’s a good maverick along with me now.

speaker: Moderator
text: All right. Let’s go another subject. Lead question, two minutes to you, senator McCain. Much has been said about the lessons of Vietnam. What do you see as the lessons of Iraq?

speaker: John McCain
text: I think the lessons of Iraq are very clear that you cannot have a failed strategy that will then cause you to nearly lose a conflict. Our initial military success, we went in to Baghdad and everybody celebrated. And then the war was very badly mishandled. I went to Iraq in 2003 and came back and said, we’ve got to change this strategy. This strategy requires additional troops, it requires a fundamental change in strategy and I fought for it. And finally, we came up with a great general and a strategy that has succeeded.

speaker: John McCain
text: And I want to tell you that now that we will succeed and our troops will come home, and not in defeat, that we will see a stable ally in the region and a fledgling democracy.

speaker: Moderator
text: Two minutes, how you see the lessons of Iraq, Senator Obama.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, this is an area where Senator McCain and I have a fundamental difference because I think the first question is whether we should have gone into the war in the first place.

speaker: Moderator
text: Do you agree with that, the lesson of Iraq?

speaker: John McCain
text: The next president of the United States is not going to have to address the issue as to whether we went into Iraq or not. The next president of the United States is going to have to decide how we leave, when we leave, and what we leave behind. That’s the decision of the next president of the United States.

speaker: Moderator
text: Well, let’s go at some of these things…

speaker: John McCain
text: Senator Obama is the chairperson of a committee that oversights NATO that’s in Afghanistan. To this day, he has never had a hearing.

speaker: Moderator
text: What about that point?

speaker: John McCain
text: I mean, it’s remarkable.

speaker: Moderator
text: All right. What about that point?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Which point? He raised a whole bunch of them.

speaker: Moderator
text: I know, OK, let’s go to the latter point and we’ll back up. The point about your not having been…

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Look, I’m very proud of my vice presidential selection, Joe Biden, who is the chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and as he explains, and as John well knows, the issues of Afghanistan, the issues of Iraq, critical issues like that, don’t go through my subcommittee because they’re done as a committee as a whole.

speaker: Moderator
text: Senator Obama…

speaker: Barack Obama
text: … of judgment, of whether or not — of whether or not — if the question is who is best-equipped as the next president to make good decisions about how we use our military, how we make sure that we are prepared and ready for the next conflict, then I think we can take a look at our judgment.

speaker: Moderator
text: I have got a lot on the plate here…

speaker: John McCain
text: I’m afraid Senator Obama doesn’t understand the difference between a tactic and a strategy. But the important — I’d like to tell you, two Fourths of July ago I was in Baghdad. General Petraeus invited Senator Lindsey Graham and me to attend a ceremony where 688 brave young Americans, whose enlistment had expired, were reenlisting to stay and fight for Iraqi freedom and American freedom.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: That’s not true.

speaker: John McCain
text: They just passed an electoral…

speaker: Barack Obama
text: That’s not true.

speaker: John McCain
text: An election law just in the last few days. There is social, economic progress, and a strategy, a strategy of going into an area, clearing and holding, and the people of the country then become allied with you. They inform on the bad guys. And peace comes to the country, and prosperity.

speaker: Moderator
text: Let me see…

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Jim, Jim, this is a big…

speaker: John McCain
text: It was a strategy. And that same strategy will be employed in Afghanistan by this great general. And Senator Obama, who after promising not to vote to cut off funds for the troops, did the incredible thing of voting to cut off the funds for the troops in Iraq and Afghanistan.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Jim, there are a whole bunch of things we have got to answer. First of all, let’s talk about this troop funding issue because John always brings this up. Senator McCain cut — Senator McCain opposed funding for troops in legislation that had a timetable, because he didn’t believe in a timetable.

speaker: John McCain
text: Admiral Mullen suggests that Senator Obama’s plan is dangerous for America.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: That’s not the case.

speaker: John McCain
text: That’s what …

speaker: Barack Obama
text: What he said was a precipitous…

speaker: John McCain
text: That’s what Admiral Mullen said.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: … withdrawal would be dangerous. He did not say that. That’s not true.

speaker: John McCain
text: And also General Petraeus said the same thing. Osama bin Laden and General Petraeus have one thing in common that I know of, they both said that Iraq is the central battleground.

speaker: John McCain
text: It didn’t exceed beyond mine, because I know that that’s a strategy that has worked and can succeed. But if we snatch defeat from the jaws of victory and adopt Senator Obama’s plan, then we will have a wider war and it will make things more complicated throughout the region, including in Afghanistan.

speaker: Moderator
text: Afghanistan, lead — a new — a new lead question. Now, having resolved Iraq, we’ll move to Afghanistan.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Yes, I think we need more troops. I’ve been saying that for over a year now.

speaker: Moderator
text: Afghanistan, Senator McCain?

speaker: John McCain
text: First of all, I won’t repeat the mistake that I regret enormously, and that is, after we were able to help the Afghan freedom fighters and drive the Russians out of Afghanistan, we basically washed our hands of the region.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Nobody talked about attacking Pakistan. Here’s what I said.

speaker: John McCain
text: I — I don’t think that Senator Obama understands that there was a failed state in Pakistan when Musharraf came to power. Everybody who was around then, and had been there, and knew about it knew that it was a failed state.

speaker: John McCain
text: A war that I was in, where we had an Army, that it wasn’t through any fault of their own, but they were defeated. And I know how hard it is for that — for an Army and a military to recover from that. And it did and we will win this one and we won’t come home in defeat and dishonor and probably have to go back if we fail.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Jim, let me just make a point. I’ve got a bracelet, too, from Sergeant – from the mother of Sergeant Ryan David Jopeck (ph), given to me in green bay. She asked me, can you please make sure another mother is not going through what I’m going through.

speaker: John McCain
text: You might think that with that kind of concern that Senator Obama would have gone to Afghanistan, particularly given his responsibilities as a subcommittee chairman. By the way, when I’m subcommittee chairman, we take up the issues under my subcommittee. But the important thing is — the important thing is I visited Afghanistan and I traveled to Waziristan and I traveled to these places and I know what our security requirements are. I know what our needs are. So the point is that we will prevail in Afghanistan, but we need the new strategy and we need it to succeed.

speaker: Moderator
text: I have some good news and bad news for the two of you. You all are even on time, which is remarkable, considering we’ve been going at it …

speaker: Barack Obama
text: A testimony to you, Jim.

speaker: Moderator
text: I don’t know about that. But the bad news is all my little five minute things have run over, so, anyhow, we’ll adjust as we get there. But the amount of time is even.

speaker: John McCain
text: My reading of the threat from Iran is that if Iran acquires nuclear weapons, it is an existential threat to the State of Israel and it is a threat to other countries in the region because the other countries in the region will feel compelling requirement to acquire nuclear weapons as well.

speaker: Moderator
text: Two minutes on Iran, Senator Obama.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, let me just correct something very quickly. I believe the Republican Guard of Iran is a terrorist organization. I’ve consistently said so. What Senator McCain refers to is a measure in the Senate that would try to broaden the mandate inside of Iraq. To deal with Iran.

speaker: Moderator
text: Senator, what about talking?

speaker: John McCain
text: Senator Obama twice said in debates he would sit down with Ahmadinejad, Chavez and Raul Castro without precondition. Without precondition. Here is Ahmadinenene (ph), Ahmadinejad, who is, Ahmadinejad, who is now in New York, talking about the extermination of the State of Israel, of wiping Israel off the map, and we’re going to sit down, without precondition, across the table, to legitimize and give a propaganda platform to a person that is espousing the extermination of the state of Israel, and therefore then giving them more credence in the world arena and therefore saying, they’ve probably been doing the right thing, because you will sit down across the table from them and that will legitimize their illegal behavior.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: So let’s talk about this. First of all, Ahmadinejad is not the most powerful person in Iran. So he may not be the right person to talk to. But I reserve the right, as president of the United States to meet with anybody at a time and place of my choosing if I think it’s going to keep America safe.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Senator McCain mentioned Henry Kissinger, who’s one of his advisers, who, along with five recent secretaries of state, just said that we should meet with Iran — guess what — without precondition. This is one of your own advisers.

speaker: John McCain
text: Of course.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: If we can’t meet with our friends, I don’t know how we’re going to lead the world in terms of dealing with critical issues like terrorism.

speaker: John McCain
text: I’m not going to set the White House visitors schedule before I’m president of the United States. I don’t even have a seal yet.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Of course not.

speaker: John McCain
text: He said that there could be secretary-level and lower level meetings. I’ve always encouraged them. The Iranians have met with Ambassador Crocker in Baghdad.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Look, I mean, Senator McCain keeps on using this example that suddenly the president would just meet with somebody without doing any preparation, without having low-level talks. Nobody’s been talking about that, and Senator McCain knows it. This is a mischaracterization of my position.

speaker: John McCain
text: So let me get this right. We sit down with Ahmadinejad, and he says, “We’re going to wipe Israel off the face of the Earth,” and we say, “No, you’re not”? Oh, please.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: No, let me tell…

speaker: John McCain
text: By the way, my friend, Dr. Kissinger, who’s been my friend for 35 years, would be interested to hear this conversation and Senator Obama’s depiction of his — of his positions on the issue. I’ve known him for 35 years.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: We will take a look.

speaker: John McCain
text: And I guarantee you he would not — he would not say that presidential top level.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Nobody’s talking about that.

speaker: John McCain
text: Of course he encourages and other people encourage contacts, and negotiations, and all other things. We do that all the time.

speaker: Moderator
text: We’re going to go to a new…

speaker: John McCain
text: And Senator Obama is parsing words when he says precondition means preparation.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I am not parsing words.

speaker: John McCain
text: He’s parsing words, my friends.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I’m using the same words that your advisers use.

speaker: Moderator
text: New lead question.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, I think that, given what’s happened over the last several weeks and months, our entire Russian approach has to be evaluated, because a resurgent and very aggressive Russia is a threat to the peace and stability of the region.

speaker: Moderator
text: Two minutes on Russia, Senator McCain.

speaker: John McCain
text: Well, I was interested in Senator Obama’s reaction to the Russian aggression against Georgia. His first statement was, “Both sides ought to show restraint.”

speaker: John McCain
text: And they showed solidarity with them, but, also, they are very concerned about the Russian threats to regain their status of the old Russian to regain their status of the old Russian empire.

speaker: Moderator
text: You see any — do you have a major difference with what he just said?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: No, actually, I think Senator McCain and I agree for the most part on these issues. Obviously, I disagree with this notion that somehow we did not forcefully object to Russians going into Georgia.

speaker: Moderator
text: We’ve got time for one more lead question segment. We’re way out of…

speaker: Moderator
text: Quick response and then…

speaker: John McCain
text: No one from Arizona is against solar. And Senator Obama says he’s for nuclear, but he’s against reprocessing and he’s against storing. So…

speaker: Barack Obama
text: That’s just not true, John. John, I’m sorry, but that’s not true.

speaker: John McCain
text: … it’s hard to get there from here. And off-shore drilling is also something that is very important and it is a bridge.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I just have to respond very quickly, just to correct — just to correct the record.

speaker: John McCain
text: So I want to say that, with the Nunn-Lugar thing…

speaker: Moderator
text: Excuse me, Senator.

speaker: John McCain
text: … I supported Nunn-Lugar back in the early 1990s when a lot of my colleagues didn’t. That was the key legislation at the time and put us on the road to eliminating this issue of nuclear waste and the nuclear fuel that has to be taken care of.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I — I just have to correct the record here. I have never said that I object to nuclear waste. What I’ve said is that we have to store it safely.

speaker: Moderator
text: All right.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: I’ve got to make this point, Jim.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: He objects…

speaker: John McCain
text: I have voted for alternate fuel all of my time…

speaker: Barack Obama
text: He — he — he objects…

speaker: Moderator
text: One at a time, please.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: He objected…

speaker: Moderator
text: One at a time.

speaker: John McCain
text: No one can be opposed to alternate energy.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: All right, fair enough. Let’s move on. You’ve got one more energy — you’ve got one more question.

speaker: Moderator
text: This is the last — last lead question. You have two minutes each. And the question is this, beginning with you, Senator McCain.

speaker: John McCain
text: I think it’s much less than it was the day after 9/11. I think it — that we have a safer nation, but we are a long way from safe.

speaker: Moderator
text: Two minutes, Senator Obama.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, first of all, I think that we are safer in some ways. Obviously, we’ve poured billions of dollars into airport security. We have done some work in terms of securing potential targets, but we still have a long way to go.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: And this is the greatest country on Earth. But because of some of the mistakes that have been made — and I give Senator McCain great credit on the torture issue, for having identified that as something that undermines our long-term security — because of those things, we, I think, are going to have a lot of work to do in the next administration to restore that sense that America is that shining beacon on a hill.

speaker: Moderator
text: Do you agree there’s much to be done in a new administration to restore…

speaker: John McCain
text: But in the case of missile defense, Senator Obama said it had to be, quote, “proven.” That wasn’t proven when Ronald Reagan said we would do SDI, which is missile defense. And it was major — a major factor in bringing about the end of the Cold War.

speaker: Moderator
text: You see the same connections that Senator McCain does?

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Oh, there’s no doubt. Look, over the last eight years, this administration, along with Senator McCain, have been solely focused on Iraq. That has been their priority. That has been where all our resources have gone.

speaker: John McCain
text: I’ve been involved, as I mentioned to you before, in virtually every major national security challenge we’ve faced in the last 20-some years. There are some advantages to experience, and knowledge, and judgment.

speaker: Barack Obama
text: Well, let me just make a closing point. You know, my father came from Kenya. That’s where I get my name.

speaker: Moderator
text: Few seconds. We’re almost finished.

speaker: John McCain
text: Jim, when I came home from prison, I saw our veterans being very badly treated, and it made me sad. And I embarked on an effort to resolve the POW-MIA issue, which we did in a bipartisan fashion, and then I worked on normalization of relations between our two countries so that our veterans could come all the way home.

speaker: Moderator
text: And that ends this debate tonight.

speaker: Raddatz
text: it was a pre-planned assault by heavily armed men. Wasn’t this a massive intelligence failure, Vice President Biden?

speaker: Joe Biden
text: What is was, it was a tragedy, Martha. It — Chris Stevens was one of our best. We lost three other brave Americans.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Congressman Ryan?

speaker: Ryan
text: We mourn the loss of these four Americans who were murdered.

speaker: Ryan
text: When you take a look at what has happened just in the last few weeks, they sent the U.N. ambassador out to say that this was because of a protest and a YouTube video. It took the president two weeks to acknowledge that this was a terrorist attack.

speaker: Ryan
text: This Benghazi issue would be a tragedy in and of itself, but unfortunately it’s indicative of a broader problem. And that is what we are watching on our TV screens is the unraveling of the Obama foreign policy, which is making the (inaudible) more chaotic us less safe.

speaker: Raddatz
text: I just want to you about right in the middle of the crisis. Governor Romney, and you’re talking about this again tonight, talked about the weakness; talked about apologies from the Obama administration. Was that really appropriate right in the middle of the crisis?

speaker: Ryan
text: On that same day, the Obama administration had the exact same position. Let’s recall that they disavowed their own statement that they had put out earlier in the day in Cairo. So we had the same position, but we will — it’s never too early to speak out for our values.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: With all due respect, that’s a bunch of malarkey.

speaker: Raddatz
text: And why is that so?

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Because not a single thing he said is accurate. First of all…

speaker: Raddatz
text: Be specific.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: I will be very specific. Number one, the — this lecture on embassy security — the congressman here cut embassy security in his budget by $300 million below what we asked for, number one. So much for the embassy security piece.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Can we talk — let me go back to Libya.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Yeah, sure.

speaker: Raddatz
text: What were you first told about the attack? Why — why were people talking about protests? When people in the consulate first saw armed men attacking with guns, there were no protesters. Why did that go on (inaudible)?

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Because that was exactly what we were told by the intelligence community. The intelligence community told us that. As they learned more facts about exactly what happened, they changed their assessment. That’s why there’s also an investigation headed by Tom Pickering, a leading diplomat from the Reagan years, who is doing an investigation as to whether or not there are any lapses, what the lapses were, so that they will never happen again.

speaker: Raddatz
text: And they wanted more security there.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Well, we weren’t told they wanted more security there. We did not know they wanted more security again. And by the way, at the time we were told exactly — we said exactly what the intelligence community told us that they knew. That was the assessment. And as the intelligence community changed their view, we made it clear they changed their view.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Mr. Ryan, I want to ask you about — the Romney campaign talks a lot about no apologies. He has a book called called “No Apologies.” Should the U.S. have apologized for Americans burning Korans in Afghanistan? Should the U.S. apologize for U.S. Marines urinating on Taliban corpses?

speaker: Ryan
text: Oh, gosh, yes. Urinating on Taliban corpses? What we should not apologize for…

speaker: Raddatz
text: Burning Korans, immediately?

speaker: Ryan
text: What — what we should not be apologizing for are standing up for our values. What we should not be doing is saying to the Egyptian people, while Mubarak is cracking down on them, that he’s a good guy and, in the next week, say he ought to go.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Let’s move to Iran. I’d actually like to move to Iran, because there’s really no bigger national security…

speaker: Ryan
text: Absolutely.

speaker: Raddatz
text: … this country is facing. Both President Obama and Governor Romney have said they will prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, even if that means military action. Last week, former Defense Secretary Bob Gates said a strike on Iran’s facilities would not work and, quote, “could prove catastrophic, haunting us for generations.” Can the two of you be absolutely clear and specific to the American people how effective would a military strike be? Congressman Ryan?

speaker: Ryan
text: We cannot allow Iran to gain a nuclear weapons capability. Now, let’s take a look at where we’ve gone — come from. When Barack Obama was elected, they had enough fissile material — nuclear material to make one bomb. Now they have enough for five. They’re racing toward a nuclear weapon. They’re four years closer toward a nuclear weapons capability.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Vice President Biden?

speaker: Joe Biden
text: It’s incredible. Look, imagine had we let the Republican Congress work out the sanctions. You think there’s any possibility the entire world would have joined us, Russia and China, all of our allies? These are the most crippling sanctions in the history of sanctions, period. Period.

speaker: Ryan
text: We want to prevent war.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: And the interesting thing is, how are they going to prevent war? How are they going to prevent war if they say there’s nothing more that we — that they say we should do than what we’ve already done, number one.

speaker: Ryan
text: Martha? Let’s…

speaker: Raddatz
text: Congressman Ryan? RYAN: Let’s look at this from the view of the ayatollahs. What do they see? They see this administration trying to water down sanctions in Congress for over two years. They’re moving faster toward a nuclear weapon. They’re spinning the centrifuges faster.

speaker: Raddatz
text: How do you do it so quickly? Look, you — you both saw Benjamin Netanyahu hold up that picture of a bomb with a red line and talking about the red line being in spring. So can you solve this, if the Romney-Ryan ticket is elected, can you solve this in two months before spring and avoid nuclear — nuclear…

speaker: Ryan
text: We can debate a time line. We can debate the time line, whether there’s — it’s that short a time or longer. I agree that it’s probably longer.

speaker: Raddatz
text: You don’t agree with that bomb and whether the Israelis…

speaker: Ryan
text: I don’t want to go into classified stuff. But we both agree that to do this peacefully you’ve got to get them to change their minds. They’re not changing their minds. And look at what this administration…

speaker: Raddatz
text: But what — what do…

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Let me tell you what the ayatollah sees.

speaker: Ryan
text: You have to have credibility.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: The ayatollah sees his economy being crippled. The ayatollah sees that there are 50 percent fewer exports of oil. He sees the currency going into the tank. He sees the economy going into freefall. And he sees the world for the first time totally united in opposition to him getting a nuclear weapon.

speaker: Raddatz
text: What does that mean, a bunch of stuff?

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Well, it means it’s simply inaccurate.

speaker: Ryan
text: It’s Irish.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: It — it is.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Thanks for the translation. OK.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: We Irish call it malarkey. But last thing. The secretary of defense has made it absolutely clear, we didn’t walk anything back. We will not allow the Iranians to get a nuclear weapon. What Bibi held up there was when they get to the point where they can enrich uranium enough to put into a weapon. They don’t have a weapon to put it into.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Congressman Ryan?

speaker: Joe Biden
text: I don’t know what world this guy’s living in. RYAN: Thank heavens we had these sanctions in place. It’s in spite of their opposition.

speaker: Ryan
text: They’ve given 20 waivers to this sanction. And all I have to point to are the results. They’re four years closer toward a nuclear weapon. I think that case speaks for itself.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Can you tell the American people…

speaker: Joe Biden
text: By the way, they…

speaker: Raddatz
text: What’s worse, another war in the Middle East…

speaker: Joe Biden
text: … they are not four years closer to a nuclear weapon.

speaker: Ryan
text: Of course they are.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: They’re — they’re closer to being able to get enough fissile material to put in a weapon if they had a weapon.

speaker: Raddatz
text: You are acting a little bit like they don’t want one.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Oh, I didn’t say — no, I’m not saying that. But facts matter, Martha. You’re a foreign policy expert. Facts matter. All this loose talk about them, “All they have to do is get to enrich uranium in a certain amount and they have a weapon,” not true. Not true.

speaker: Raddatz
text: What about Bob Gates’ statement? Let me read that again, “could prove catastrophic, haunting us for generations.”

speaker: Joe Biden
text: He is right. It could prove catastrophic, if we didn’t do it with precision.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Congressman Ryan?

speaker: Ryan
text: And what it does is it undermines our credibility by backing up the point when we make it that all options are on the table. That’s the point. The ayatollahs see these kinds of statements and they think, “I’m going to get a nuclear weapon.”

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Martha, let me tell you what Russia…

speaker: Raddatz
text: Well, let me ask you what’s worse, war in the Middle East, another war in the Middle East, or a nuclear-armed Iran?

speaker: Ryan
text: I’ll tell you what’s worse. I’ll tell you what’s worse.

speaker: Ryan
text: A nuclear-armed Iran which triggers a nuclear arms race in the Middle East. This is the world’s largest sponsor of — of terrorism. They’ve dedicated themselves…

speaker: Ryan
text: … to wiping an entire country off the map. They call us the Great Satan. And if they get nuclear weapons, other people in the neighborhood will pursue their nuclear weapons, as well.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Vice President Biden?

speaker: Ryan
text: We can’t live with that.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: War should always be the absolute last resort. That’s why these crippling sanctions, which Bibi Netanyahu says we should continue, which — if I’m not mistaken — Governor Romney says we — we should continue. I may be mistaken. He changes his mind so often, I could be wrong.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Gentlemen, I want to bring the conversation to a different kind of national security issue, the state of our economy. The number-one issue here at home is jobs. The percentage of unemployed just fell below 8 percent for the first time in 43 months. The Obama administration had projected that it would fall below 6 percent now after the addition of close to a trillion dollars in stimulus money.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: I don’t know how long it will take. We can and we will get it under 6 percent. Let’s look at — let’s take a look at the facts. Let’s look at where we were when we came to office. The economy was in free fall. We had — the great recession hit; 9 million people lost their job; $1.7 — $1.6 trillion in wealth lost in equity in your homes, in retirement accounts for the middle class.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: They’re pushing the continuation of a tax cut that will give an additional $500 billion in tax cuts to 120,000 families. And they’re holding hostage the middle class tax cut because they say we won’t pass — we won’t continue the middle class tax cut unless you give the tax cut for the super wealthy.

speaker: Ryan
text: Joe and I are from similar towns. He’s from Scranton, Pennsylvania. I’m from Janesville, Wisconsin. You know what the unemployment rate in Scranton is today?

speaker: Joe Biden
text: I sure do.

speaker: Ryan
text: It’s 10 percent.

speaker: Ryan
text: You know what it was the day you guys came in — 8.5 percent.

speaker: Ryan
text: That’s how it’s going all around America.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: You don’t read the statistics. That’s not how it’s going. It’s going down.

speaker: Raddatz
text: (inaudible) two-minute answer (inaudible)

speaker: Ryan
text: Look, did they come in and inherit a tough situation? Absolutely. But we’re going in the wrong direction. Look at where we are. The economy is barely limping along. It’s growing a 1.3 percent. That’s slower than it grew last year and last year was slower than the year before.

speaker: Ryan
text: He talks about Detroit. Mitt Romney’s a car guy. They keep misquoting him, but let me tell you about the Mitt Romney I know. speaker: Joe Biden
text: But I always say what I mean. And so does Romney.

speaker: Ryan
text: We want everybody to succeed. We want to get people out of poverty, in the middle class, onto a life of self-sufficiently. We believe in opportunity and upward mobility. That’s what we’re going to push for in a Romney administration.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Vice president? I have a feeling you have a few things to say here.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: The idea — if you heard that — that little soliloquy on 47 percent and you think he just made a mistake, then I think you’re — I — I think — I got a bridge to sell you.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Congressman Ryan?

speaker: Ryan
text: Let’s not forget that they came in with one-party control. When Barack Obama was elected, his party controlled everything. They had the ability to do everything of their choosing. And look at where we are right now.

speaker: Raddatz
text: When could you get it below 6 percent?

speaker: Ryan
text: That’s what our entire premise of our pro-growth plan for a stronger middle class is all about: getting the economy growing at 4 percent, creating 12 million jobs over the next four years.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Go ahead. Go ahead.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Martha, look. His colleague…

speaker: Ryan
text: Crony capitalism and corporate welfare.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: … runs an investigative committee, spent months and months and months going into this.

speaker: Ryan
text: This is the — this is the inspector general.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Months and months. They found no evidence of cronyism.

speaker: Raddatz
text: You did ask for stimulus money, correct?

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Sure he did. By the way…

speaker: Ryan
text: On two occasions we — we — we advocated for constituents who were applying for grants. That’s what we do. We do that for all constituents who are…

speaker: Ryan
text: Was it a good idea to spend taxpayer dollars on electric cars in Finland, or on windmills in China?

speaker: Ryan
text: Was it a good idea to borrow all this money from countries like China and spend it on all these various different interest groups?

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Let me tell you what was a good idea. It was a good idea, Moody’s and others said that this was exactly what we needed to stop this from going off the cliff. It set the conditions to be able to grow again. We have, in fact, 4 percent of those green jobs didn’t go under — went under, didn’t work. It’s a better batting average than investment bankers have. They have about a 40 percent…

speaker: Ryan
text: Where are the 5 million green jobs that were being…

speaker: Raddatz
text: I want to move on here to Medicare and entitlements. I think we’ve gone over this quite enough.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: By the way, any letter you send me, I’ll entertain.

speaker: Ryan
text: I appreciate that, Joe.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Let’s talk about Medicare and entitlements. Both Medicare and Social Security are going broke and taking a larger share of the budget in the process.

speaker: Ryan
text: Absolutely. Medicare and Social Security are going bankrupt. These are indisputable facts.

speaker: Ryan
text: And then they put this new Obamacare board in charge of cutting Medicare each and every year in ways that will lead to denied care for current seniors.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Vice President Biden, two minutes.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: You know, I heard that death panel argument from Sarah Palin. It seems every vice presidential debate I hear this kind of stuff about panels.

speaker: Ryan
text: Here’s the problem. They got caught with their hands in the cookie jar, turning Medicare into a piggybank for Obamacare. Their own actuary from the administration came to Congress and said one out of six hospitals and nursing homes are going to go out of business as a result of this.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: That’s not what they said.

speaker: Ryan
text: 7.4 million seniors are projected to lose their current Medicare Advantage coverage they have. That’s a $3,200 benefit cut.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: That didn’t happen.

speaker: Ryan
text: What we’re saying…

speaker: Joe Biden
text: More people signed up.

speaker: Ryan
text: These are from your own actuaries.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: More — more — more people signed up for Medicare Advantage after the change.

speaker: Ryan
text: What — there’s…

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Nobody is…

speaker: Ryan
text: Mr. Vice President, I know…

speaker: Joe Biden
text: No, this is…

speaker: Ryan
text: Mr. Vice President, I know you’re under a lot of duress to make up for lost ground, but I think people would be better served if we don’t keep interrupting each other.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Well, don’t take all the four minutes then.

speaker: Ryan
text: Let me just — let me just say this. We are not — we’re saying don’t change benefits for people 55 and above. They already organized their retirement around these promises.

speaker: Ryan
text: … programs for those of us.

speaker: Raddatz
text: But let — let me ask you this. What — what is your specific plan for seniors who really can’t afford to make up the difference in the value of what you call a premium support plan and others call a voucher?

speaker: Ryan
text: Hundred percent coverage…

speaker: Ryan
text: That’s what we’re saying. So we’re saying…

speaker: Raddatz
text: How do you make that up?

speaker: Ryan
text: … income adjusts (inaudible) these premium support payments by taking down the subsidies for wealthy people.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: There’s not one Democrat who endorses it.

speaker: Ryan
text: It’s a plan…

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Not one Democrat who (inaudible).

speaker: Ryan
text: Our partner is a Democrat from Oregon.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: And he said he does no longer support (inaudible).

speaker: Ryan
text: We — we — we put it — we put it together with the former Clinton budget director.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Who disavows it.

speaker: Ryan
text: This idea — this idea came from the Clinton commission to save Medicare chaired by Senator John Breaux.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Which was rejected.

speaker: Ryan
text: If we don’t — if we don’t fix this problem pretty soon then current seniors get cut. Here’s the problem: 10,000 people are retiring every single day in America today and they will for 20 years. That’s not a political thing, that’s a math thing.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Martha, if we just did one thing, if we just — if they just allowed Medicare to bargain for the cost of drugs like Medicaid can, that would save $156 billion right off the bat.

speaker: Ryan
text: And it would deny seniors choices.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: All — all — all…

speaker: Ryan
text: It has a restricted…

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Seniors are not denied.

speaker: Ryan
text: Absolutely.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: They are not denied.

speaker: Ryan
text: Because it’s working well right now.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Because we’ve changed the law.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Vice President Biden, let me ask you, if it could help solve the problem, why not very slowly raise the Medicare eligibility age by two years, as Congressman Ryan suggests?

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Look, I was there when we did that with Social Security in 1983. I was one of eight people sitting in the room that included Tip O’Neill negotiating with President Reagan. We all got together and everybody said, as long as everybody’s in the deal, everybody’s in the deal, and everybody is making some sacrifice, we can find a way.

speaker: Ryan
text: A voucher is you go to your mailbox, get a check, and buy something. Nobody’s proposing that. Barack Obama four years ago running for president said if you don’t have any fresh ideas, use stale tactics to scare voters. If you don’t have a good record to run on, paint your opponent as someone people should run from.

speaker: Ryan
text: Make a big election about small ideas.

speaker: Raddatz
text: You were one of the few lawmakers to stand with President Bush when he was seeking to partially privatize Social Security.

speaker: Ryan
text: For younger people. What we said then, and what I’ve always agreed is let younger Americans have a voluntary choice of making their money work faster for them within the Social Security system.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: You saw how well that worked.

speaker: Ryan
text: That’s not what Mitt Romney’s proposing. What we’re saying is no changes for anybody 55 and above.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: What Mitt Romney is proposing…

speaker: Ryan
text: And then the kinds of changes we’re talking about for younger people like myself is don’t increase the benefits for wealthy people as fast as everybody else. Slowly raise the retirement age over time.

speaker: Ryan
text: It wouldn’t get to the age of 70 until the year 2103 according to the actuaries.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Quickly, Vice President?

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Quickly. The bottom line here is that all the studies show that if we went with Social Security proposal made by Mitt Romney, if you’re 40 — in your 40s now you will pay $2,600 a year — you get $2,600 a year less in Social Security. If you’re in your 20s now, you get $4,700 (inaudible) less.

speaker: Ryan
text: That statistic was completely misleading. But more importantly…

speaker: Joe Biden
text: That’s — there are the facts right…

speaker: Ryan
text: This is what politicians do when they don’t have a record to run on: try to scare people from voting for you. If you don’t get ahead of this problem, it’s going to…

speaker: Joe Biden
text: Medicare beneficiaries — there are more beneficiaries…

speaker: Raddatz
text: We’re going to — we’re going to move…

speaker: Raddatz
text: … very simple question…

speaker: Ryan
text: We’re not going to run away. Medicare and Social Security did so much for my own family. We are not going to jeopardize this program, but we have to save it…

speaker: Joe Biden
text: You are jeopardizing this program. You’re changing the program from a guaranteed benefit to premium support. Whatever you call it, the bottom line is people are going to have to pay more money out of their pocket and the families I know and the families I come from, they don’t have the money to pay more out…

speaker: Ryan
text: That’s why we’re saying more for lower income people and less for higher income people.

speaker: Raddatz
text: Gentlemen, I would like to move on to a very simple question for both of you, and something tells me I won’t get a very simple answer, but let me ask you this.

speaker: Joe Biden
text: I gave you a simple answer. He’s raising the cost of Medicare.

speaker: Raddatz
